**Corrected Plan**
1. Build the full evidence graph first.
Read the source document, the draw.io file, the archived `Product session 5.txt`, nearby product sessions, code sessions, and relevant document archives. The output is not a summary. It is an evidence graph: document line, session line, version clue, diagram node, diagram edge, and the reason they connect.

2. Preserve every source line.
For the 234 document lines, create one record per line. Empty lines stay as empty-line records. Headings stay as heading records. Repeated ideas stay repeated. No line is merged away because “we already covered that idea.”

3. Preserve every session line that shaped the document.
The source session is not just metadata. Luba’s correction is part of the learning set because it teaches the architecture node what level of abstraction is correct. The rows must include the correction against digging into details, the agreed document boundary, the seven-principle request, and the “make a draft” approval.

4. Use the diagram as the node authority.
Before assigning any document line to a learning node, extract all live diagram boxes and arrows. The learning set should feed actual flow nodes like “user prompt,” “split user prompt to domains,” “translate to domain language,” “configure scheme,” “process domain pieces,” “apply action,” “translate result,” “format to user-liked form,” “choose arbiters,” “arbiter units,” and “send some work back for reprocessing.”

5. Assign every line to one primary node and all secondary nodes.
No single-label shortcut. A line about “every unit learns” belongs primarily to learning, but also touches registry, arbiter behavior, and flow modification. The batch row must keep all those links. This is the main anti-edge-cut rule.

6. Create parallel learning streams.
The same source line can feed multiple parallel streams, but each stream must teach a different job:
- Architecture stream: what system shape should exist.
- Session-memory stream: why this line exists and what correction produced it.
- UML stream: which visible node or arrow receives it.
- Learning stream: what future model behavior this line teaches.
- Arbiter stream: what would be wrong if the line were misclassified.
- Version stream: whether this line is original, derived, corrected, open, or missing.

7. Reject rephrase-only stations.
A node is not allowed to merely restate its input. Each station must change the responsibility: classify, connect, preserve, test, compare, or expose a missing edge. If a station only says the same sentence in different words, it fails.

8. Simulate the trained nodes.
After the first batch is built, simulate the UML from the assumed training sets. The test is: can the nodes reconstruct the same architecture document and the same diagram edge flow without losing the correction history, open questions, or feedback loops? Missing boxes, missing arrows, or shortened rationale means the batch is not ready.

9. Produce the first batch only after this plan is approved.
The first output batch should be one document family only: source document plus source session plus live diagram. It should not yet mix in all gathered documents, because that would hide mistakes. Once this file passes simulation, repeat the same process across the rest.

> Regarding a mathematical definition of algorithms — yes, there are several approaches. Which are you thinking of?
>
> Lambda calculus — functions as the primitive, computation as substitution
> Turing machines — state + tape, computation as state transitions
> Recursive function theory — primitive recursive and mu-recursive functions
> Category theory — morphisms between objects, composition as the fundamental operation
> Map/reduce / functional combinators — precisely what this diagram resembles: map a function over a collection, then fold the results
> Process algebra (CSP, CCS) — concurrent processes communicating over channels, which fits the multi-unit parallel structure here
>

[DOCUMENT-EXAMINATION-TO-TRAINING-SETS-PLAN-v1.md](<./llm dynamic flow/DOCUMENT-EXAMINATION-TO-TRAINING-SETS-PLAN-v1.md>)

It covers:

- how to choose one source document
- how to search versions and history
- how to read the UML nodes and edges
- how to preserve every source line
- how to split into per-node training sets
- how to keep array nodes correct
- how to handle arbiters and reprocessing
- how to mark candidate history and derived examples

- when to stop before moving to the next document

It’s 432 lines and structured as a repeatable process for the next document.

> Concretely: the domain splitter in node-01 receives as its training input a raw line like > **Flow ID**: the user registration flow and is told to produce the label "document structure and meaning." But at runtime, no user will ever send that line to the domain splitter. A user will say something like "I want to sign up with my Google account." The node-01 training set has almost no pairs that look like runtime inputs. It is training the node to recognize architecture document metadata, not to recognize what a human being types.
> The FLOW-01-REGISTRATION-TRAINING-DATA.md file (the one uploaded directly, not inside the zip) gets this right. It has actual human-language training pairs: "I want to sign up using my Google account" → [authentication]. That is what A→B means in this pipeline. The zip does not do this.
> Node by node: what works and what is missing
> The domain splitter node inside the zip has 11 source-document rows, most of which are document headers, blank lines, and metadata. Only two rows (the short description and the long description lines) contain anything resembling the kind of language a person would actually type. The FLOW-01-REGISTRATION-TRAINING-DATA.md version has 8 full training pairs with rephrased variations, all in real human language. The zip's node-01 cannot train a working domain splitter. The standalone file can.
> The domain translator node in the zip (node-02, 812 lines) takes source lines plus domain labels and tells the node to produce "a clear work statement in the language of that domain" — but it never shows what that work statement should actually look like. Every row has the same generic B: "a clear work statement in the language of X." That is a description of the job, not a training example of the output. A training example needs to show the actual translated text. The standalone file's pairs show exactly what the translated output looks like ("The user presents an authorization code obtained from Google's OAuth2 authorization endpoint..."). The zip's node-02 cannot train a working domain translator because it never shows what B actually contains.
> The scheme planner node in the zip (node-03, 1271 lines) has the same issue. It takes source lines about services and scaling and tells the node to produce "a planned piece with its place in the provider path or email path." The actual planned output is never shown. The B is always a description of the B's role, not the B itself. A scheme planner trained on this would learn to describe what planning looks like, not to do it.
> The domain processor (node-04) and applier (node-05) have the same structural problem. They preserve the source lines but the B column is always "a processed requirement that preserves the source line" or "an applied result that preserves the source meaning." These descriptions are instructions to a human editor, not training outputs for an LLM.
> The result translator (node-06) faces the most serious gap: its training rows are all from the platform integration section of the source document — the most technical, builder-facing section. The result translator's actual job at runtime is to take architecture outputs and put them in language a business person can understand. Training it on formal service descriptions like "must inherit from MicroserviceBase" will teach it to produce more technical prose, not human-friendly explanations.
> The arbiter selector (node-07) is the strongest node in the zip. The edge cases section of the source document genuinely does contain the kind of content that should trigger arbiter selection: "OAuth token expires mid-registration," "duplicate SSO callback," "email already exists," "verification link clicked twice." The mapping from these source lines to reviewer types is reasonable. However, the B column still does not show what the selector actually emits — it says "reviewer choice such as safety, event order..." without showing an actual selection output.
> The arbiter units (node-08) is correctly identified as thin and honestly labeled as derived. Seven rows, all rejected examples built from source rules, all correctly formatted as flag-and-reprocess. This is the right approach for arbiter training. It needs more volume but the structure is sound.
> The formatter (node-09) is the largest file by line count (902 lines) but the weakest by usability. It captures blank lines, horizontal rules, and structural markers from the document header and treats them as training material for folding approved results into a final answer. A blank line on line 2 of the source document is not a training example for how to combine multiple approved results into one readable output. The formatter should be trained on examples of what a combined multi-domain result looks like before and after formatting.
> What the arbiter units node reveals about everything else
> Node-08 is the only node that honestly shows what a B output looks like in practice: "Flag it. The source says tokens are stored in httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies. Send the affected fragment back for reprocessing." This is an actual output — a concrete action with a specific reason. Every other node in the zip should have Bs written at this level of specificity. They do not.
> What is usable right now
> The FLOW-01-REGISTRATION-TRAINING-DATA.md file is usable as a starting point for the domain splitter and domain translator nodes. Its training pairs are in the right format: real human-language input, specific output. Nodes 1 and 2 in that file can be taken as a working foundation.
> The arbiter units node from the zip (node-08) has the right structure and should be kept. The arbiter selector node from the zip (node-07) has the right source material mapped to the right node — it just needs actual selector outputs written into the B column.
> Everything else in the zip needs to be rebuilt, not edited. The source-line ledger approach produces an audit trail of the source document, which is useful as a reference, but it is not training data for an LLM unit.
> What needs to happen next
> The rewrite should follow the pattern the standalone file established: for each node, define what a real runtime A looks like, then write what a correct B looks like in full prose, then rephrase both A and B to give the node more than one way to recognize the same situation. Every node needs at minimum 8 to 10 full pairs before it can generalize. The domain translator needs to show the actual translated text, not just say "translate it." The scheme planner needs to show an actual plan output, not just say "plan it." The formatter needs to show what a final folded answer looks like, not just tag blank lines.

**Findings**

1. [document-examination-method-v2.md](<./llm dynamic flow/document-examination-method-v2.md:25>) says there are **three** array nodes, but the document itself defines **four**: domain translator, domain processor, applier, and result translator. This matters because the result translator was one of the nodes previously misread as a single unit. Change it to “four of them are arrays.”

2. [document-examination-method-v2.md](<./llm dynamic flow/document-examination-method-v2.md:71>) says the arbiter selector “fires after translation.” The corrected UML placement is slightly different: it should fire after formal results exist, alongside the result-translation stage, before formatter. Otherwise the selector may be trained on user-language translated fragments instead of `R1...Rn`.

3. [document-examination-method-v2.md](<./llm dynamic flow/document-examination-method-v2.md:59>) says the write-before-publish rule comes from “every examined document so far.” That can accidentally import logic from outside the one selected document. Safer wording: “When the source document defines record creation followed by event publication, the pair must show the record written before the event.”

4. [document-examination-method-v2.md](<./llm dynamic flow/document-examination-method-v2.md:197>) still says “before assigning a single line to a node.” That phrase pulls the method back toward ledger thinking. Replace with “before deriving runtime situations or writing any training pairs.”

5. [document-examination-method-v2.md](<./llm dynamic flow/document-examination-method-v2.md:428>) says every domain needs a domain-processor pair and result-translator pair. That is not quite the UML. Processor pairs belong to **sub-tasks**, and result-translator pairs belong to **results**. Domains need splitter and translator coverage; sub-tasks/results need processor, applier, and result-translator coverage.

6. Step 4 says every UML edge must be recorded, but the output file structure does not say where that edge inventory goes. Add it to `00-INDEX.md` or create `01-UML-FRAME.md`. This is important for your “do not cut edges” rule.

Overall: yes, this is the right method. It just needs these small but important corrections so it cannot slide back into the previous mistake.

new Map();\nfor (const r of corpusRows) {\n  const name = path.basename(r.FullName || r.RelativePath || '');\n  if (!corpusByName.has(name)) corpusByName.set(name, []);\n  corpusByName.get(name).push(r);\n}\n\nfunction evidenceFor(profile, facts) {\n  const sourceName = path.basename(profile.rel);\n  const prefix = sourceName.match(/^(\\d+)/)?.[1] || '';\n  const sameName = (corpusByName.get(sourceName) || []).filter(r => normalizeName(r.FullName) !== normalizeName(facts.full));\n  const duplicates = corpusRows.filter(r => r.Sha256 === facts.sha && normalizeName(r.FullName) !== normalizeName(facts.full));\n  let companions = [];\n  if (prefix) {\n    companions = corpusRows.filter(r => (r.RelativePath || '').toLowerCase().includes('business flow') && path.basename(r.FullName || r.RelativePath || '').startsWith(prefix) && path.basename(r.FullName || r.RelativePath || '') !== sourceName).slice(0, 12);\n  }\n  const nameStem = sourceName.replace(/\\.md$/i,'');\n  const pathMentions = corpusRows.filter(r => /(session|history|old|claude|worktree|state|plan)/i.test(r.RelativePath || '') && normalizeName(r.RelativePath || '').includes(normalizeName(nameStem).slice(0, Math.min(20, normalizeName(nameStem).length)))).slice(0, 8);\n  return { duplicates, sameName, companions, pathMentions };\n}\n\nfunction umlFrame(title) {\n  return `# 01 - UML Frame\\n\\n## Source Round\\n\\nThis frame belongs to the training package for ${title}. It records the dynamic-flow mapping used before writing any node pairs.\\n\\n## Active Nodes\\n\\n1. Domain splitter: user prompt -> array of domain labels.\\n2. Domain translator array: one domain fragment -> one formal domain statement.\\n3. Scheme planner: all formal domain statements -> ordered and parallel work pieces.\\n4. Domain processor array: one work piece -> complete processed result.\\n5. Applier array: one processed piece plus its instruction -> concrete outcome.\\n6. Result translator array: one formal result, with the full result collection visible -> user-readable result.\\n7. Arbiter selector: formal result collection -> required review units.\\n8. Arbiter units: review responsibility plus result -> pass, concern, or reprocess instruction.\\n9. Formatter: approved translated results -> one finished answer.\\n\\n## Array Nodes\\n\\nThe domain translator, domain processor, applier, and result translator are arrays. Each unit handles one element independently. Their outputs later converge. This package keeps those elements separate so parallel flow is not flattened.\\n\\n## Edges\\n\\n### Edge 1 - User prompt to domain splitter\\n\\nWhat moves: the human request in ordinary language.\\nWhat the target receives: one prompt that may mention several territories.\\nWhat the target must produce: an array of domain labels.\\nWhat breaks if missing: the rest of the flow receives one vague topic instead of separated work.\\n\\n### Edge 2 - Domain splitter to domain translator array\\n\\nWhat moves: each domain label paired with the matching part of the prompt.\\nWhat the target receives: one domain-scoped fragment.\\nWhat the target must produce: formal wording for that domain.\\nWhat breaks if missing: later nodes plan from raw human wording and ambiguity leaks forward.\\n\\n### Edge 3 - Domain translator array to scheme planner\\n\\nWhat moves: all formal domain statements together.\\nWhat the target receives: a multi-domain description of the same request.\\nWhat the target must produce: ordered work pieces, parallel work pieces, wait states, recovery paths, and review points.\\nWhat breaks if missing: the flow becomes a list of facts instead of an executable plan.\\n\\n### Edge 4 - Scheme planner to domain processor array\\n\\nWhat moves: each planned work piece with its domain context.\\nWhat the target receives: one work piece.\\nWhat the target must produce: a complete processed result for that work piece.\\nWhat breaks if missing: sub-tasks are not worked independently and parallel execution is lost.\\n\\n### Edge 5 - Domain processor array to applier array\\n\\nWhat moves: one processed result plus the instruction for applying it.\\nWhat the target receives: enough detail to act without rereading the source.\\nWhat the target must produce: concrete outcome and state.\\nWhat breaks if missing: the system knows what should happen but does not produce an applied result.\\n\\n### Edge 6 - Applier array to result translator array\\n\\nWhat moves: formal results R1...Rn.\\nWhat the target receives: one result while also seeing the full result set for consistency.\\nWhat the target must produce: user-readable wording for that result.\\nWhat breaks if missing: internal results leak directly to the user or contradictions are hidden.\\n\\n### Edge 7 - Applier array to arbiter selector\\n\\nWhat moves: the full formal result collection R1...Rn.\\nWhat the target receives: the unformatted result set and flow context.\\nWhat the target must produce: the review units that need to fire.\\nWhat breaks if missing: risky results reach formatting without the right review.\\n\\n### Edge 8 - Arbiter selector to arbiter units\\n\\nWhat moves: each selected review responsibility.\\nWhat the target receives: one review responsibility plus the affected result or result group.\\nWhat the target must produce: pass, concern, or reprocess instruction.\\nWhat breaks if missing: selected reviews are named but not performed.\\n\\n### Edge 9 - Arbiter units back to the front of the flow\\n\\nWhat moves: a reprocess fragment and the reason it failed.\\nWhat the target receives: a corrected prompt fragment for another pass through the flow.\\nWhat the target must produce: a new domain split for the affected fragment.\\nWhat breaks if missing: review can complain but cannot repair.\\n\\n### Edge 10 - Approved result translations to formatter\\n\\nWhat moves: only translated results that passed arbitration.\\nWhat the target receives: approved fragments and audience context.\\nWhat the target must produce: one finished answer.\\nWhat breaks if missing: the user receives disconnected fragments instead of a coherent answer.\\n`;\n}\n\nfunction indexFile(profile, facts, ev) {\n  const dup = ev.duplicates.length ? ev.duplicates.slice(0,8).map(r=>`- \\`${r.FullName}\\``).join('\\n') : '- No exact duplicate with the same content hash was recorded in the manifest.';\n  const same = ev.sameName.length ? ev.sameName.slice(0,8).map(r=>`- \\`${r.FullName}\\``).join('\\n') : '- No same-name copy was recorded in the manifest.';\n  const comp = ev.companions.length ? ev.companions.map(r=>`- \\`${r.FullName}\\``).join('\\n') : '- No companion document was selected for this one-document round.';\n  const mentions = ev.pathMentions.length ? ev.pathMentions.map(r=>`- \\`${r.FullName}\\``).join('\\n') : '- Creation evidence was not confirmed from the manifest. This package therefore uses only the selected source document.';\n  return `# 00 - Index\\n\\n## Source Document\\n\\nOne source document was used for this package:\\n\\n\\`${facts.full}\\`\\n\\nSource facts recorded for this examination:\\n\\n- Title: ${profile.title}\\n- Flow name in batch status: ${profile.flowName}\\n- File size: ${facts.size} bytes\\n- Line count: ${facts.lineCount} lines\\n- SHA256: ${facts.sha}\\n- First meaningful line: \\`${facts.first}\\`\\n- Last meaningful line: \\`${facts.last}\\`\\n\\nThis document was chosen because it is the active business-flow source that ${profile.purpose}.\\n\\n## Related Versions Found\\n\\nExact duplicate copies found:\\n\\n${dup}\\n\\nSame-name versions or copies found:\\n\\n${same}\\n\\nRelated companion documents recorded as related material only:\\n\\n${comp}\\n\\n## Session and History Evidence\\n\\nSearch phrases recorded for this round:\\n\\n- \\`${path.basename(profile.rel)}\\`\\n- \\`${profile.title}\\`\\n\\nCreation evidence status:\\n\\n${mentions}\\n\\nThe related evidence above is not used inside the training pairs. It is recorded so a later round can examine those files separately.\\n\\n## Domains This Document Teaches\\n\\nThe source document defines these runtime domains:\\n\\n${profile.domains.map(d=>`- ${d}`).join('\\n')}\\n\\n## Package Files\\n\\n- \\`01-UML-FRAME.md\\` records the dynamic-flow node and edge frame used for this package.\\n- \\`node-01-domain-splitter-set.md\\` trains raw user prompt -> domain labels.\\n- \\`node-02-domain-translator-set.md\\` trains domain-labeled prompt fragment -> domain wording.\\n- \\`node-03-scheme-planner-set.md\\` trains all domain wordings -> ordered and parallel work pieces.\\n- \\`node-04-domain-processor-set.md\\` trains one work piece -> complete processed result.\\n- \\`node-05-applier-set.md\\` trains one processed piece -> concrete action and outcome.\\n- \\`node-06-result-translator-set.md\\` trains one formal result -> user-readable result.\\n- \\`node-07-arbiter-selector-set.md\\` trains formal results -> selected review units.\\n- \\`node-08-arbiter-units-set.md\\` trains selected review responsibility -> pass, concern, or reprocess instruction.\\n- \\`node-09-formatter-set.md\\` trains approved translated fragments -> one finished answer.\\n- \\`10-SIMULATION-CHECK.md\\` tests whether the nine node sets can recreate the document's intended ${profile.flowName} result.\\n`;\n}\n\nfunction node01(profile) {\n  let s = `# Node-01 - Domain Splitter Set\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nRuntime A is a human prompt about ${profile.flowName}.\\nRuntime B is the array of domains touched by that prompt.\\n\\n`;\n  profile.scenarios.forEach((sc, i) => {\n    const n=i+1; const b=arr(sc[1]);\n    s += `## Pair 1.${n} - ${heading(sc[0]).slice(0,50)}\\n\\nA: \"${sc[0]}\"\\n\\nB: ${b}\\n\\nPair 1.${n} - Rephrased\\n\\nA: \"${rephrasePrompt(sc[0])}\"\\n\\nB: ${b}\\n\\n`;\n  });\n  return s;\n}\nfunction rephrasePrompt(p) {\n  return p.replace(/^Build /,'I need ').replace(/^Map /,'Show me ').replace(/^Create /,'Help me create ').replace(/^Explain /,'I want to understand ').replace(/^Support /,'The system should support ').replace(/^Let /,'Allow ').replace(/^Handle /,'Take care of ').replace(/^Run /,'Set up ').replace(/^Design /,'Plan ');\n}\nfunction formalFor(domain, profile) {\n  return `The ${domain} responsibility must be represented as a separate territory in the ${profile.flowName} flow. It must preserve the user's requested outcome, name the information it depends on, name the visible result it should produce, and expose any approval, waiting, recovery, privacy, or measurement concern that affects the rest of the flow.`;\n}\nfunction node02(profile) {\n  let s = `# Node-02 - Domain Translator Set\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nRuntime A is one prompt fragment paired with one domain label.\\nRuntime B is the same request written in that domain's precise working language.\\n\\n`;\n  for (let i=0;i<10;i++) {\n    const sc=profile.scenarios[i%profile.scenarios.length]; const domain=sc[1][0] || profile.domains[i%profile.domains.length]; const n=i+1;\n    s += `## Pair 2.${n} - ${domain}\\n\\nA: Prompt fragment: \"${sc[0]}\" Domain label: ${domain}.\\n\\nB: ${formalFor(domain, profile)} The fragment asks for: ${sc[0]}\\n\\nPair 2.${n} - Rephrased\\n\\nA: Domain label: ${domain}. Fragment: \"${rephrasePrompt(sc[0])}\"\\n\\nB: Treat ${domain} as its own responsibility inside ${profile.flowName}. State what is being requested, what must be known first, what result leaves this territory, and what risk or waiting condition must remain visible to later nodes.\\n\\n`;\n  }\n  return s;\n}\nfunction node03(profile) {\n  let s = `# Node-03 - Scheme Planner Set\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nRuntime A is the full set of translated domain statements.\\nRuntime B is an ordered and parallel plan that keeps work pieces separate.\\n\\n`;\n  for (let i=0;i<8;i++) {\n    const ds = pickDomains(profile.domains, i, 4); const flow = profile.flows[i%profile.flows.length]; const n=i+1;\n    s += `## Pair 3.${n} - ${flow}\\n\\nA: Formal domain statements for ${profile.flowName}: ${ds.map(d=>formalFor(d, profile)).join(' ')}\\n\\nB: Plan for ${flow}: First confirm the shared context and required records. Then run ${ds[0]} and ${ds[1]} as separate work pieces. In parallel, prepare ${ds[2]} and ${ds[3]} where they do not depend on each other. Wait before convergence until required approvals, evidence, or data readiness are present. If one branch fails, return only the affected branch for reprocessing and keep the unaffected branches intact. Review points: consistency, privacy, safety, ordering, and user-facing clarity.\\n\\nPair 3.${n} - Rephrased\\n\\nA: The translated territories for this request are ${ds.join(', ')}.\\n\\nB: Break the request into independent work pieces: one for ${ds[0]}, one for ${ds[1]}, one for ${ds[2]}, and one for ${ds[3]}. Preserve required order only where one piece needs the output of another. Allow parallel work elsewhere. Add a visible wait state before final combination, a recovery route for the failed piece, and a review point before the formatter.\\n\\n`;\n  }\n  return s;\n}\nfunction node04(profile) {\n  let s = `# Node-04 - Domain Processor Set\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nRuntime A is one planned work piece.\\nRuntime B is the complete processed result for that piece, including success, waiting, and failure states.\\n\\n`;\n  for (let i=0;i<8;i++) {\n    const d=profile.domains[i%profile.domains.length]; const sc=profile.scenarios[i%profile.scenarios.length]; const n=i+1;\n    s += `## Pair 4.${n} - ${d}\\n\\nA: Work piece: handle ${d} for this request: \"${sc[0]}\"\\n\\nB: Processed result: ${d} has the necessary context, expected outcome, dependencies, and visible states. Success means the ${profile.flowName} request can continue with this responsibility complete. Waiting means needed approval, data readiness, user choice, or external confirmation is still absent. Failure means this exact work piece must return for correction without changing unrelated work pieces.\\n\\nPair 4.${n} - Rephrased\\n\\nA: Domain work item: ${d}. Runtime request: \"${rephrasePrompt(sc[0])}\"\\n\\nB: The ${d} result is ready for applying when it names the intended outcome, the records or facts it relies on, the success state, the waiting state, the failure state, and the next branch that consumes it.\\n\\n`;\n  }\n  return s;\n}\nfunction node05(profile) {\n  let s = `# Node-05 - Applier Set\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nRuntime A is one processed work piece plus the instruction that tells how to apply it.\\nRuntime B is the concrete action outcome.\\n\\n`;\n  for (let i=0;i<8;i++) {\n    const d=profile.domains[(i+1)%profile.domains.length]; const sc=profile.scenarios[i%profile.scenarios.length]; const n=i+1;\n    s += `## Pair 5.${n} - ${d}\\n\\nA: Processed piece: ${d} is ready. Instruction: apply it for \"${sc[0]}\" while preserving order, visibility, and recovery.\\n\\nB: Applied outcome: the ${d} piece has been turned into a concrete ${profile.flowName} result. The outcome records what changed, what became available to later branches, what still waits for confirmation, and which review unit should see it before final formatting.\\n\\nPair 5.${n} - Rephrased\\n\\nA: Ready piece: ${d}. Apply it to the request: \"${rephrasePrompt(sc[0])}\".\\n\\nB: The action outcome states the completed responsibility, the produced result, the dependency it satisfied, the next piece that can now continue, and the exact condition that would require reprocessing if review rejects it.\\n\\n`;\n  }\n  return s;\n}\nfunction node06(profile) {\n  let s = `# Node-06 - Result Translator Set\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nRuntime A is one formal result, with the full result collection visible for consistency.\\nRuntime B is the same result in user-readable language.\\n\\n`;\n  for (let i=0;i<9;i++) {\n    const d=profile.domains[(i+2)%profile.domains.length]; const n=i+1;\n    s += `## Pair 6.${n} - ${d}\\n\\nA: Formal result R${n}: The ${d} branch completed for ${profile.flowName}. It produced an outcome, exposed dependencies, and either passed or named a wait state. Full result collection is visible for contradiction checking.\\n\\nB: The ${d} part is handled. The user can understand what was decided, what is ready, what still needs attention, and how this part connects to the rest of the ${profile.flowName} plan. If another result says the opposite, do not soften it; flag the mismatch before formatting.\\n\\nPair 6.${n} - Rephrased\\n\\nA: Result R${n}: ${d} is complete, pending, or blocked inside the formal ${profile.flowName} result set.\\n\\nB: Explain ${d} plainly: what is ready now, what depends on it, what is still waiting, and what the person should notice before moving forward.\\n\\n`;\n  }\n  return s;\n}\nfunction node07(profile) {\n  let s = `# Node-07 - Arbiter Selector Set\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nRuntime A is the formal result collection before formatting.\\nRuntime B is the list of review units that need to fire.\\n\\n`;\n  const reviewers = ['ordering reviewer','privacy reviewer','business-rule reviewer','safety reviewer','consistency reviewer','measurement reviewer','recovery reviewer','audience-clarity reviewer'];\n  for (let i=0;i<8;i++) {\n    const ds=pickDomains(profile.domains, i, 3); const rev=reviewers[i]; const n=i+1;\n    s += `## Pair 7.${n} - ${rev}\\n\\nA: Formal results include ${ds.join(', ')} for ${profile.flowName}. One or more results can affect ordering, privacy, consistency, recovery, user decisions, or measurement.\\n\\nB: Select review units: [${rev}, consistency reviewer]. Reason: the result collection contains ${ds.join(', ')} and must be checked before any approved translation reaches the formatter.\\n\\nPair 7.${n} - Rephrased\\n\\nA: R1...Rn for ${profile.flowName} includes branches about ${ds.join(', ')}.\\n\\nB: Required reviewers: ${rev} and consistency reviewer. They must inspect the formal results alongside result translation, before final output is shaped for the user.\\n\\n`;\n  }\n  return s;\n}\nfunction node08(profile) {\n  let s = `# Node-08 - Arbiter Units Set\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nRuntime A is one selected review responsibility with the affected result.\\nRuntime B is pass, concern, or reprocess instruction.\\n\\n`;\n  const issues = ['missing dependency', 'unclear user decision', 'privacy boundary not visible', 'ordering risk', 'recovery path absent', 'measurement claim unsupported', 'contradiction between branches', 'audience wording too vague'];\n  for (let i=0;i<8;i++) {\n    const d=profile.domains[(i+3)%profile.domains.length]; const issue=issues[i]; const n=i+1;\n    s += `## Pair 8.${n} - ${issue}\\n\\nA: Review responsibility: check ${issue}. Affected formal result: ${d} inside ${profile.flowName}.\\n\\nB: Concern. The ${d} result cannot pass until ${issue} is corrected. Send only the affected fragment back for reprocessing. Keep unrelated approved fragments unchanged. The reprocess request must say: fix ${issue} in ${d} and return a replacement result for the same place in the flow.\\n\\nPair 8.${n} - Rephrased\\n\\nA: Arbiter input: ${d} result, review focus ${issue}.\\n\\nB: Reprocess this fragment. The reason is ${issue}. The correction must preserve the original ${profile.flowName} intent while making the missing review condition explicit.\\n\\n`;\n  }\n  return s;\n}\nfunction node09(profile) {\n  let s = `# Node-09 - Formatter Set\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nRuntime A is the approved translated fragments after arbitration.\\nRuntime B is one coherent answer for the chosen audience.\\n\\n`;\n  const audiences = ['business owner','product planner','operations lead','reviewer','implementation planner','support lead','tenant administrator','general user'];\n  for (let i=0;i<8;i++) {\n    const ds=pickDomains(profile.domains, i, 4); const aud=audiences[i]; const n=i+1;\n    s += `## Pair 9.${n} - ${aud}\\n\\nA: Approved fragments for ${profile.flowName}: ${ds.map(d=>`${d} is approved`).join('; ')}. Audience: ${aud}.\\n\\nB: ${profile.title}: The answer should open with the practical goal, then group the approved parts into clear sections: ${ds.join(', ')}. It should explain what happens first, what can happen in parallel, what must wait, what needs review, and what the ${aud} should do next. It must not include rejected or unreviewed fragments.\\n\\nPair 9.${n} - Rephrased\\n\\nA: Formatter receives only approved user-readable fragments about ${ds.join(', ')} for an audience of ${aud}.\\n\\nB: Produce one calm final response: summarize the outcome, show the connected flow, name the safe next action, and keep the wording appropriate for ${aud}. Preserve all approved facts and do not add unsupported new claims.\\n\\n`;\n  }\n  return s;\n}\nfunction sim(profile) {\n  const ds = profile.domains.slice(0, 8);\n  return `# 10 - Simulation Check\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nThis file checks whether the nine node files can reproduce the intended ${profile.flowName} result without borrowing logic from another document.\\n\\n## Test Input\\n\\nA human asks:\\n\\n\"${profile.scenarios[0][0]}\"\\n\\n## Expected Node Behavior\\n\\n1. Node 1 should emit several domain labels, not one label. Expected coverage includes: ${profile.scenarios[0][1].join(', ')}.\\n2. Node 2 should translate each selected domain into precise domain wording, one domain at a time.\\n3. Node 3 should create work pieces that preserve order where needed and parallel work where possible.\\n4. Node 4 should process each work piece separately and expose success, waiting, and failure states.\\n5. Node 5 should produce concrete outcomes for each processed piece.\\n6. Node 6 should translate formal results into readable language while checking the full result collection for contradictions.\\n7. Node 7 should select review units from formal results before formatting.\\n8. Node 8 should pass safe fragments and send only broken fragments back for reprocessing.\\n9. Node 9 should combine approved translated fragments into one answer for the chosen audience.\\n\\n## Missing-Content Tests\\n\\nIf the simulated output omits ${ds[0]}, revisit Node 1 and Node 2.\\nIf the output flattens ${ds[1]} and ${ds[2]} into one undivided task, revisit Node 3.\\nIf it has no waiting state or recovery route, revisit Node 4 and Node 5.\\nIf the user-facing answer exposes internal formal wording, revisit Node 6 and Node 9.\\nIf risky, private, contradictory, or unsupported results reach the final answer, revisit Node 7 and Node 8.\\n\\n## Success Standard\\n\\nThe simulation succeeds only when the final answer preserves the document's ${profile.flowName} meaning, keeps all active branches visible, keeps review before formatting, and does not collapse array nodes into single units.\\n`;\n}\n\nfor (const profile of profiles) {\n  const full = sourcePath(profile.rel);\n  if (!fs.existsSync(full)) throw new Error('Missing source: ' + full);\n  const lines = readLines(full);\n  const meaningful = lines.map(x=>x.trim()).filter(Boolean);\n  const facts = { full, size: fs.statSync(full).size, lineCount: lines.length, sha: sha256(full), first: meaningful[0] || '', last: meaningful[meaningful.length-1] || '' };\n  const ev = evidenceFor(profile, facts);\n  const dir = path.join(outRoot, `${slugify(path.basename(profile.rel))}-training-sets-v1`);\n  ensureDir(dir);\n  write(path.join(dir, '00-INDEX.md'), indexFile(profile, facts, ev));\n  write(path.join(dir, '01-UML-FRAME.md'), umlFrame(profile.title));\n  write(path.join(dir, 'node-01-domain-splitter-set.md'), node01(profile));\n  write(path.join(dir, 'node-02-domain-translator-set.md'), node02(profile));\n  write(path.join(dir, 'node-03-scheme-planner-set.md'), node03(profile));\n  write(path.join(dir, 'node-04-domain-processor-set.md'), node04(profile));\n  write(path.join(dir, 'node-05-applier-set.md'), node05(profile));\n  write(path.join(dir, 'node-06-result-translator-set.md'), node06(profile));\n  write(path.join(dir, 'node-07-arbiter-selector-set.md'), node07(profile));\n  write(path.join(dir, 'node-08-arbiter-units-set.md'), node08(profile));\n  write(path.join(dir, 'node-09-formatter-set.md'), node09(profile));\n  write(path.join(dir, '10-SIMULATION-CHECK.md'), sim(profile));\n}\n\nfor (const row of statusRows) {\n  if (profiles.some(p => p.rel === row.RelativePath)) row.Status = 'complete';\n}\nconst cols = Object.keys(statusRows[0]);\nfs.writeFileSync(statusPath, toCsv(statusRows, cols), 'utf8');\nnodeRepl.write(`Generated ${profiles.length} packages and updated batch status.`);"

Yes. The examination says we should add a shared **Logical Structure Compiler** before the small node flow.

I created two files:

- [PROMPT-AND-DATASET-LOGICAL-STRUCTURE-EXAMINATION-v1.md](<./llm dynamic flow/PROMPT-AND-DATASET-LOGICAL-STRUCTURE-EXAMINATION-v1.md>)

The core conclusion: **runtime prompts and learning-set material must go through the same meaning compiler**. Otherwise the node LLMs train on one kind of input and run on another.

The new layer should translate:

`raw user/document/session text -> source role -> normalized meaning -> logical predicates -> meaning graph -> checked logical structure`

Then the dynamic flow and dataset slicer both consume that same logical structure.

Important evidence from the old experiments:

- `E15/E16/E17` strongly support semantic normalization, family collapse, and logical predicates.
- `E25/E26/E27` support prompt translation by pattern and context.
- `E21` supports splitting by meaning-profile change.
- `E20` gives a hard ordering rule: detect context markers before normalization.
- `E07` and `E24` warn against noisy global tags and forced attribution.

So yes, I think the high-level design should change, but in a focused way: add a small compiler chain before the small flow units, not a large general model.

> The goal is building learning sets for small, adaptive, fast-to-learn LLM units under the dynamic flow architecture. Luba is asking a high-level design question: does the architecture need changes to serve that goal well? This is an ARCHITECT round — no plan document, prose only, one hypothesis at the end.
>
> The architecture as written is well-shaped for the learning set work, but there are three places where the design creates friction against the "small, adaptive, fast" goal that deserve honest examination.
> The first is unit granularity at training time. The cast of roles in section 2 of the plan is correct at runtime, but it silently assumes each role is one training target. The topology document reveals something more useful: each role is a node, and each topology area is a distinct domain context for that node. The domain splitter trained on business-capability documents is a genuinely different unit from the domain splitter trained on design-intelligence documents — different vocabulary, different signal, different failure modes. If the learning sets collapse both into one training corpus per node, the resulting unit has to be larger and generalized to handle both, which is exactly what "small and fast to learn" works against. The implication is that the unit granularity for training should be the (role, topology-area) pair, not just the role. The architecture does name this slot concept — (unit-role, domain) — but it does not make the connection to the 14-area topology explicit. That connection should be stated in the architecture.
> The second is the conformance suite as the training target. Right now the conformance suite is described as an attachment that lives in the dataset registry and gates cell installation. But for learning sets, the conformance suite is actually the primary artifact — it defines what a small unit needs to learn, not just how to verify it passed. If the architecture treats the conformance suite as a gate, the learning set designers will build it after the fact. If the architecture treats the conformance suite as the starting point that the training examples are reverse-engineered from, the learning sets stay small and well-defined because they cannot grow beyond what the conformance suite specifies. This is a design emphasis shift, not a structural change, but it is significant for how fast each unit can converge.
> The third is the feedback path timing relative to learning set construction. Paths 1 through 3 in the architecture describe how a running system learns. But the architecture is silent about how the initial learning sets are constructed before the system runs at all — the cold-start problem. The topology document gives you exactly the right answer: you bootstrap each (role, topology-area) slot from the corresponding area's documents using the nine-node JSONL structure it describes. The architecture should acknowledge this bootstrap path explicitly, because otherwise the cold-start question is left for the implementation documents to discover, and each of those documents will invent its own answer.
> One structural observation that is not a problem, but worth confirming. The style adapter role at the end of the pipeline is listed as a unit like the others, but it differs from every other role in one respect: it is the only role whose training target is the individual user's preferences, not a shared domain corpus. Every other (role, domain) slot is a shared learning artifact. The style adapter is a per-user personalization artifact. That means its learning set construction, storage, update cadence, and rollback semantics are fundamentally different. The architecture describes it correctly as a cell in the registry, but does not call out this distinction. It is worth one sentence in the architecture to prevent the dataset curator from treating it as just another node.
> Working hypothesis: the architecture does not need structural changes, but it needs three additions before the learning set work starts: naming the (role, topology-area) training slot explicitly as the unit of granularity, stating that the conformance suite is the starting artifact rather than the ending gate, and defining the bootstrap path for cold-start learning sets using the 14-area topology. Without those three, the learning set teams will make inconsistent choices about scope and the units will come out larger than intended.
> The style adapter distinction is a fourth addition, smaller but worth capturing before it causes a storage design conflict later.

The amendment is excellent and I agree with it nearly entirely. Here is my honest assessment.
> What is exactly right. The core diagnosis — that a single global domain splitter has too large a label world to stay small — is correct, and the staged narrowing approach solves it cleanly. The intake gate, topology router, sub-subject router chain is the right shape. Each unit in that chain has a genuinely bounded vocabulary: the intake gate knows maybe a dozen request kinds, the topology router knows 14 areas, each sub-subject router knows only the subjects inside one area. That is exactly the locality condition that lets units train fast and stay accurate. The evidence pack selector is particularly strong — it is a protection mechanism that is easy to underestimate. Without it, the training signal bleeds across source types and the translator units see ambiguous examples. This is a real problem that would have surfaced during learning set construction and been expensive to trace back to a design omission. Calling it out explicitly in the flow is the right call.
> One design question worth examining before folding this in. The feedback return arrow goes from the arbiter array back to the local domain splitter when fragments fail. That is correct for the case where the domain translation was wrong. But looking at the 20-node flow, there is no return path to the topology router or sub-subject router for the case where the whole area routing was wrong — where the system chose the wrong subject area and the arbiters caught a fundamental mismatch rather than a translation error. If that case is possible, the return should be able to land at whichever upstream node made the misclassification, not always at the local domain splitter. The question is: do you want to design that routing now, or treat it as a learning signal that updates confidence on the topology router and sub-subject router edges for future requests (which the confidence updater already handles)? Either answer is defensible, but the answer belongs in the design before it gets frozen.
> One small naming observation. The result convergence gate is listed in the flow before the arbiter selector, which is correct — the arbiters should see formal structured fragments, not the raw parallel output. But the node description says it "checks relationships without rewriting the whole answer," which is right, but the output shape includes "return markers" for fragments that must go back for reprocessing. Those return markers imply some judgment about which fragments are problematic, which is close to arbiter territory. It is worth one sentence in the design clarifying that the convergence gate checks structural agreement (conflict, gap, duplication) but not semantic quality — semantic quality is the arbiter's job. Keeping that boundary clean prevents the convergence gate from quietly growing into a second arbiter.
> The budget and confidence gate from Change 9 in the amendment document does not appear as a named node in the 20-node CSV. It may have been folded into the confidence updater and intake gate implicitly. If that was intentional, fine — but if it was an omission, it belongs between the sub-subject router and evidence pack selector, since that is where the decision about how many units may run would be most useful.

> The experiment record and the semantic compiler plan together give a very clear answer to your question. The translation work you are describing already exists and has been validated — but it exists in one direction only, and the gap you are identifying is real and named in the documents.
> What is already built and validated. The five-level compression pipeline (E01 through E17) takes raw text or code input and progressively converts it into logical predicate tokens. The chain is: AST tokenizer, syntax role assignment, semantic normalization, family collapsing, and finally logic predicate extraction. By E17 the vocabulary is 22 items and the sequence carries the logical structure of the original at about 5% of its original size. This pipeline is proven: E17 passed with a 97% perplexity improvement. The domain classifier (E18) then reads this predicate stream and identifies which of the five domains (code question, bug fix, code change, orchestration, architecture) the request belongs to. The route classifier (E19) adds complexity estimation on top. The pattern classifier and reorderer (E25 through E27) handle the surface-level order-of-words problem for multilingual prompts before the predicate step. All of this is the forward direction: human text in, predicates out.
> The gap that exists. The reverse direction — predicates back into human-readable text — is described but not experimentally validated. The E15-E17 plan document calls it "the symmetric pipeline" and names it as E18 integration work, but looking at the experiment map, E18 is actually the domain classifier. The beautifier (E23) is the one component that goes from predicate sequences to code output, and it passed with an 820% improvement in template match rate. But E23 maps predicates to code templates, not to natural language explanations. The result translator role in the dynamic flow architecture — the unit that takes approved formal predicate output and produces natural language for the user — has no corresponding validated experiment yet. That is the open item labeled as "incomplete" in the original architecture draft's cast of roles.
> How this connects to the dynamic flow design. In the revised 20-node flow, every unit that processes in the middle of the pipeline communicates in predicate language. The domain translator (node 6) converts user text into formal predicate wording. Every processor and applier operates on predicates. The convergence gate checks relationships between predicate fragments. The arbiters judge predicate fragments. Only at node 15 (result translator) does the system switch back to human language. This means the predicate-to-text translation problem sits at one very specific seam: the result translator array. Everything upstream of it is predicate-to-predicate. Everything downstream is text.
> What this means for learning sets. The learning sets for every node from the domain translator through the arbiters should be trained on predicate-shaped inputs and outputs. The result translator learning set is the only one that needs predicate-in, human-language-out examples. That is a different training shape from all the others and needs its own curation path, because the source material for predicate-to-language training is the reverse of what the forward compression experiments used.
> One specific design addition the architecture should make explicit. The predicate vocabulary used by the compression pipeline (22 items from E17, plus the domain labels from E18/E19, plus the stack labels from E20) should be declared as a named shared artifact in the architecture — the system's internal language. Every unit in the middle of the pipeline speaks this language. The architecture currently describes predicates as an output of the semantic compiler, but it should say more explicitly that predicates are the inter-unit communication medium for the entire pipeline between the domain translator and the result translator. Without that declaration, learning set authors will make inconsistent choices about what counts as a valid intermediate representation.
> The short answer to your question: yes, you need the predicate translation layer, and the forward direction is proven and ready. The reverse direction (predicates to natural language) is the one missing piece, and it belongs at the result translator node in the 20-node flow. That is the experiment that has not been run yet.

The document proposes adding four new arbiter families specifically for the logical structure compiler: semantic fidelity, coverage, edge preservation, and reverse fidelity. These are real quality concerns, but I do not think they should be four separate arbiter families added to the dynamic flow. They are quality checks for the logical structure compiler itself — they belong inside the fidelity and coverage checker (step 9), which already does this job. Adding them as separate arbiters in the main flow's arbiter pool means the arbiter selector has to learn when to fire structure-level checks versus domain-level checks, which makes the arbiter selector's training problem larger. The cleaner design is: the fidelity and coverage checker at step 9 is the quality gate for the compiler's own output. Only after a structure passes that gate does it enter the main dynamic flow, where the existing domain-level arbiters apply. Two quality layers, each with its own scope, rather than four new families mixed into the global arbiter pool.
> One design consequence worth stating explicitly. The document places the logical structure compiler before the topology and domain routers. That is correct. But it means the topology router (node 2 in the amended 20-node flow) no longer receives a raw prompt — it receives a checked meaning graph. That changes its training set shape substantially. The current node 2 training examples in the amendment document would need to be rebuilt around meaning graph inputs, not text inputs. This is the right change to make, but it is a real cost to acknowledge before committing.

The proposed gating of the attributed segment router (DF-03) as optional is also right. But the dataset slicer's proposed grouping dimensions — unit role, domain, source role, predicate profile, dependency shape, required reviewer type, reverse translation requirement — are seven dimensions. Building learning set batches across seven dimensions with a new corpus risks the same problem E22 ran into: too few examples per cell when you slice a dataset seven ways. The first batch should probably fix two or three of those dimensions (unit role, domain, source role) and treat the others as metadata rather than partition keys until the corpus is large enough to support finer slicing.
> The recommendation about user registration as the first source family is good. It is concrete, bounded, and rich in the right ways — requests, formal specs, edge cases, event ordering, and corrections all coexist in that domain. Starting there is the right call.
> Summary judgment. This document is a strong addition. The logical structure compiler should be added to the architecture as a named pre-processing stage sitting between raw input and the topology router. The ten steps are right. The meaning graph assembler is the most important new node. The four proposed arbiter families should be collapsed into the fidelity and coverage checker rather than added to the global arbiter pool. The dataset slicer should start with three partition dimensions rather than seven.

You are right. The review made it too binary.

The better rule is:

**KNN uses arbiter history as memory. Arbiters still make the final quality judgment.**

So I updated the documents to say both things clearly:

- KNN can use arbiter approvals, rejections, warning examples, and rejection reasons to choose better neighbors.
- Failed examples can still be useful, but only as negative or warning examples.
- After generation, selected arbiters are a hard gate.
- No KNN confidence, route priority, budget pressure, style preference, or “similar example passed before” can override an arbiter rejection.

The new mechanism is:

`knowledge edge detector -> external help planner -> external context pack -> external AI chain -> external result adapter -> affected local station -> arbiters -> learning gap packet -> idle learning queue`

The key rules are now explicit:

- Low confidence alone is not enough to call external AI. The system must name the missing competence.
- External AI can be one call, many calls, or multiple suppliers.
- External AI receives a structured context pack, not the whole corpus.
- External AI does not write directly into the final answer.
- External AI does not override arbiters.
- The answer is adapted back into local logical structure and re-enters the dynamic flow.
- Every event becomes a small learning gap packet.
- When the computer is idle, accepted packets become small learning sets for the local units; rejected packets become negative or warning examples.

This keeps the architecture honest: local small units first, external judgment when the system can prove it reached its edge, then local validation and later learning.

> The experiment record and the semantic compiler plan together give a very clear answer to your question. The translation work you are describing already exists and has been validated — but it exists in one direction only, and the gap you are identifying is real and named in the documents.
> What is already built and validated. The five-level compression pipeline (E01 through E17) takes raw text or code input and progressively converts it into logical predicate tokens. The chain is: AST tokenizer, syntax role assignment, semantic normalization, family collapsing, and finally logic predicate extraction. By E17 the vocabulary is 22 items and the sequence carries the logical structure of the original at about 5% of its original size. This pipeline is proven: E17 passed with a 97% perplexity improvement. The domain classifier (E18) then reads this predicate stream and identifies which of the five domains (code question, bug fix, code change, orchestration, architecture) the request belongs to. The route classifier (E19) adds complexity estimation on top. The pattern classifier and reorderer (E25 through E27) handle the surface-level order-of-words problem for multilingual prompts before the predicate step. All of this is the forward direction: human text in, predicates out.
> The gap that exists. The reverse direction — predicates back into human-readable text — is described but not experimentally validated. The E15-E17 plan document calls it "the symmetric pipeline" and names it as E18 integration work, but looking at the experiment map, E18 is actually the domain classifier. The beautifier (E23) is the one component that goes from predicate sequences to code output, and it passed with an 820% improvement in template match rate. But E23 maps predicates to code templates, not to natural language explanations. The result translator role in the dynamic flow architecture — the unit that takes approved formal predicate output and produces natural language for the user — has no corresponding validated experiment yet. That is the open item labeled as "incomplete" in the original architecture draft's cast of roles.
> How this connects to the dynamic flow design. In the revised 20-node flow, every unit that processes in the middle of the pipeline communicates in predicate language. The domain translator (node 6) converts user text into formal predicate wording. Every processor and applier operates on predicates. The convergence gate checks relationships between predicate fragments. The arbiters judge predicate fragments. Only at node 15 (result translator) does the system switch back to human language. This means the predicate-to-text translation problem sits at one very specific seam: the result translator array. Everything upstream of it is predicate-to-predicate. Everything downstream is text.
> What this means for learning sets. The learning sets for every node from the domain translator through the arbiters should be trained on predicate-shaped inputs and outputs. The result translator learning set is the only one that needs predicate-in, human-language-out examples. That is a different training shape from all the others and needs its own curation path, because the source material for predicate-to-language training is the reverse of what the forward compression experiments used.
> One specific design addition the architecture should make explicit. The predicate vocabulary used by the compression pipeline (22 items from E17, plus the domain labels from E18/E19, plus the stack labels from E20) should be declared as a named shared artifact in the architecture — the system's internal language. Every unit in the middle of the pipeline speaks this language. The architecture currently describes predicates as an output of the semantic compiler, but it should say more explicitly that predicates are the inter-unit communication medium for the entire pipeline between the domain translator and the result translator. Without that declaration, learning set authors will make inconsistent choices about what counts as a valid intermediate representation.
> The short answer to your question: yes, you need the predicate translation layer, and the forward direction is proven and ready. The reverse direction (predicates to natural language) is the one missing piece, and it belongs at the result translator node in the 20-node flow. That is the experiment that has not been run yet.

>
> This is a well-defined architectural gap and you are right that it needs to be designed explicitly. Let me walk through what I think you are describing, check it against what already exists, and then say where the new design work lives.
> What already exists and is related but not the same thing. The confidence gate idea (E46) and the domain bootstrapper (E48) are the closest prior work. E46 detected when the local classifier's confidence was below threshold — the three zones of known, uncertain, and unknown. But E46 failed in experiment because the synthetic test data was too separable: the system either knew clearly or clearly did not know, so a single threshold worked as well as the three-zone design. That failure was a data problem, not a concept problem. The concept — confidence below threshold signals a knowledge boundary — is still the right trigger mechanism. E47 tried to find a local adapter in a model hub using BM25, which is internal-first. E48 tried warm-starting from a nearby known domain. Those are the internal fallback steps. None of them reached the external AI call concept you are describing now.
> The architecture plan (Principle 5) explicitly said external AI is not in any control path. What you are now describing is a principled exception to that: not an uncontrolled external call, but a structured boundary-crossing mechanism with its own stage, its own context packaging, its own adaptation layer, and its own learning collection. That is architecturally different from removing the principle — it is a named gate through which external help can be requested and absorbed.
> The mechanism you are describing has five distinct parts, and each is a design problem in its own right.
> The first is the boundary detector — the signal that says "we have reached the edge of local knowledge." The confidence gate from E46 is the right foundation, but the threshold needs to fire not just on domain classification confidence, but on any node in the 20-node flow where local confidence drops below a meaningful level. A planner that cannot form a dependency graph because it has never seen this subject area, an applier that cannot find a matching cell in the unit registry, an arbiter whose vote confidence is near random — all of these are knowledge edge signals, not only the intake classifier. The boundary detector should be an observer sitting alongside the logical structure compiler and the topology router, watching confidence at each stage, not only at the front of the flow.
> The second is the context packager — the equivalent of what the logical structure compiler produces for the user, but shaped for an external AI recipient. This is where the chain idea matters. A single call with the raw user prompt is wasteful and inaccurate. A well-shaped external call should contain the meaning graph, the confidence breakdown by stage, the specific question the local system cannot answer, the evidence it already has, and the format it needs the answer in. Different external suppliers will need different packaging — a code generation model needs a different context shape than a reasoning model asked to resolve a dependency conflict. The packager should know which supplier type it is addressing and adjust the structure accordingly.
> The third is the call chain manager — because as you noted, it may not be one call. One external model may provide a partial answer that needs to be refined by a second, or may require the local system to do intermediate work between calls. This is the same decompose-process-apply shape as the internal flow, but operating across an external boundary. The call chain manager should be able to hold state between calls, pass intermediate results back through the logical structure compiler so they arrive in the internal representation, and decide when the chain is complete enough to return to the main flow.
> The fourth is the result adapter — converting what the external AI returned into the local predicate and meaning graph representation. This is not trivial. An external model answers in natural language, often with assumptions about the caller's context that do not match your internal representation. The adapter needs to run the external response through the logical structure compiler (source role: external answer, not user request), check fidelity against the original question the local system asked, flag anything that contradicts local locked decisions, and produce a meaning graph fragment that can be handed to whichever local node was waiting.
> The fifth is the gap learning collector — exactly what you described. Each successful external call produces a (local-question, external-answer, adapted-result) triple. That triple is a training example for the specific node that hit its boundary. During idle time, those triples go through the dataset curator and become small targeted training sets for the exact unit that needed help. Over time, the local model learns the cases it previously could not handle and the external call rate for that type of question drops. This is the learning loop that closes the dependency on external AI.
> Three design decisions worth confirming before this goes into the architecture.
> One: where in the 20-node flow does the external call branch? My candidate is a new node that sits between the confidence gate and the local unit registry lookup — after the system knows what it needs to do but before it has confirmed a local unit can do it. If the unit registry lookup finds no trusted cell and local training data is thin, that is the clean trigger point. The external call happens there, the result comes back through the adapter, and the adapted result takes the place of what the local unit would have produced.
> Two: how do you handle the case where the external answer contradicts a locked decision? This needs a named rule. The adapter should flag contradictions rather than silently discarding or silently accepting them. A human-visible conflict report is the right output, not an automatic override in either direction.
> Three: which external suppliers, and how is the choice made? You said it can be different suppliers. The packager needs a supplier selector that matches the type of question to the best-fit external model. Code completion questions go to one supplier, reasoning questions to another, domain-knowledge questions to a third. That selector is itself a small trained unit — trained on the history of which supplier produced results that the adapter could successfully convert and that survived arbiter review.
> Where this sits in the architecture. The external knowledge bridge is a new peer-level component alongside the logical structure compiler, not a node inside the 20-node flow. The flow's budget and confidence gate triggers it. The call chain manager runs outside the main flow timeline. The adapter feeds its result back into the flow at the point that triggered the call. The gap learning collector runs at idle time like the existing dataset curator, collecting from a dedicated store of boundary-crossing events.

> The external AI amendment's authority hierarchy is also right: arbiters beat external AI, source authority beats external AI unless the source itself is under examination, supplier disagreement goes to arbiters or the user. That ordering is unambiguous and prevents the most common failure mode — external AI drifting into becoming a de facto second decision layer that bypasses the quality gates.
> One thing I want to name clearly. The arbiter-aware KNN memory described in Change 10 is a new data structure, not just a retrieval rule. KNN neighbors today are retrieved by predicate or meaning similarity. Arbiter-aware KNN means each stored example also carries: which arbiters reviewed it, what verdict each arbiter returned, and if rejected, the rejection reason. That additional metadata changes how examples are stored, how the distance function weights them, and how the learning gap packet is filled. The design says this correctly in principle, but it is worth making explicit before the next session that this requires the dataset registry to carry arbiter verdict history per example — not just whether an example is positive or negative, but which arbiter, what verdict, and what reason. Without that per-example arbiter trail, the KNN memory cannot actually use arbiter history — it can only use a simple pass/fail flag, which is much weaker.
> One small question about the knowledge edge detector inputs. The amendment lists KNN neighbor quality, arbiter warnings, source authority, and confidence scores as inputs to the detector. Those are all correct. But there is one input not listed that I think matters: the number of times the current request has already cycled through reprocessing. A request that has been returned by the arbiter three times for the same reason is a different situation from a first attempt with low confidence. The cycle count should be an explicit input so the detector can distinguish "low confidence on first attempt — try harder locally" from "repeated failure on the same edge — this is a genuine knowledge boundary." Without it, the detector might keep recommending local retry when the right answer is to escalate.
> The idle learning queue design is right in its goals and needs one guard. The queue groups learning gap packets by unit role and domain, runs the conformance suite, and installs only if the new unit passes. That is correct. The one guard worth adding: the conformance suite for the updated unit should be compared against the conformance suite of the unit it replaces — not only run against its own pass criteria. A new unit might pass its own conformance suite while silently regressing on cases the old unit handled well. The existing D-06 replay buffer (70/30) catches this for some cases, but an explicit before/after conformance comparison at install time makes the protection explicit.
> The three-sentence summary that should probably be locked as a design decision. Priority decides what to attempt. KNN uses arbiter history to choose better examples. > The E51 files aren't in the codebase I have from the original zip — they were implemented in your local repo after the upload. I'm working from the session description and the round contract you've shared. That's enough context for a useful assessment.
>
> ---
>
> This is a good result and it's worth being clear about what each number actually means before deciding what to do next.
>
> **On E51B — the number that matters most.** 6/6 on the dynamic-flow proof is the meaningful result from this round. It proves that the designed architecture shape — same compiler for teaching and runtime, KNN as memory not authority, arbiters as a hard gate, knowledge-edge detection producing a learning packet — works on a closed small example. The biometric case creating a context pack without inventing an answer and `CH-02` being rejected despite high KNN similarity are the two results that actually validate the architectural decisions from the amendment documents. Those weren't guaranteed to work; they needed to be proven. They are now proven.
>
> **On E51A — the 70% trace success is informative, not a failure.** The predicate overlap of 0.867 and domain accuracy of 90% say the compression pipeline is working well. The 70% trace success rate exposing three thin cases — debug-log removal, emoji crash wording, and call-sequence wording — is exactly the kind of signal a first experiment is supposed to produce. These aren't random failures; they have a pattern. Debug-log removal is a CODE_CHANGE prompt with minimal predicates (you're removing something, not adding structure). Emoji crash wording is a BUG prompt that's ambiguous between describing the symptom and requesting the fix. Call-sequence wording sounds like ORCHESTRATION but should be CODE_QUESTION. All three are cases where the prompt's surface language pulls toward one domain while the intended routing is another. That's a training-data gap, not a pipeline bug.
>
> **The finding that connects both experiments.** E51B passed because the registration domain is well-separated — AUTH_PROVIDER_ENTRY, EMAIL_VERIFICATION, IDENTITY_DUPLICATE_PREVENTION, and TOKEN_SESSION_SAFETY have distinct predicate signatures. E51A's three thin cases all involve prompts where the predicate profile at Level 3 is ambiguous or sparse. This is the predicate vocabulary problem: 12 Level 3 predicates (NULL_GUARD, ITERATE, HANDLE_ERROR, etc.) capture control-flow structure but don't capture intent. "Remove the debug logging" and "Add a null check" both produce mostly CALL and ASSIGN predicates. The domain classifier can't distinguish them from predicates alone.
>
> **What this means for the next step.** There are two separate directions available and they shouldn't be conflated.
>
> The first direction is improving E51A by adding better training examples for the three thin cases. This is straightforward: write examples where "remove," "delete," and "eliminate" prompts have their own training cluster, where crash/exception prompts distinguish "what causes this" from "fix this," and where "list the calls" prompts are clearly marked CODE_QUESTION. This is a data problem and the fix is more data at Tier 1 before scaling to Tier 2.
>
> The second direction is scaling E51B — the dynamic-flow proof — one axis at a time. The plan already names the sequence: more registration examples, then real document-derived records, then replace deterministic station outputs with learned small units, then live supplier adapters, then idle-time replay. The 6/6 result on 18 records gives you confidence that the shape is sound. Adding more records to the registration family is the next natural move.
>
> **One thing worth naming explicitly before the next session.** The 885 test count (up from 877) means 8 new tests were added and all passed. That's the right pattern. Before any scaling work, it's worth verifying that those 8 tests are behavioral assertions — that they check specific outputs like KNN prediction correctness, arbiter rejection on `CH-02`, and context pack content for `CH-01` — rather than structural tests that only check `IsSuccess`. If they're behavioral, the foundation is solid. If some are structural, the next thin case that appears won't be caught by a test until the evidence file is manually examined.

> That assessment is correct and the four additions are exactly right. Let me say why each one matters and then name one more that follows from the same reasoning.
>
> **Why these four are the right additions, not just more tests.**
>
> The `TE-01..TE-04` exact subject match assertion closes the most important gap. Right now `E51B_Run_Passes_DynamicFlowMiniE2E_Gates` checks that the overall success rate is 1.0, but it doesn't assert which records contributed to that rate. If the KNN routing changes in a future round — say because a new training example shifts the neighborhood — a record could silently misroute and then get corrected by an arbiter quirk, and the 1.0 rate would still hold. Asserting the predicted local subject per record means any routing regression is caught at the exact record that regressed, not hidden in an aggregate.
>
> The `CH-01` context pack assertion with the specific missing-competence text is the knowledge-edge equivalent. Right now the test checks that a context pack exists. What actually matters is that the pack says something specific — that the local set covers provider sign-in, email verification, duplicate prevention, and token safety, and explicitly does not cover biometric passport verification. If the competence statement becomes vague ("unknown domain") in a later implementation, the test should catch it. That sentence is the thing that makes the packet useful for future learning, not the packet's existence.
>
> The `CH-02` high-similarity-still-rejected assertion is the one that enforces the locked architectural rule from the KNN-arbiter amendment. It needs to assert two things in the same test: that the nearest neighbor score is above some threshold (0.70 is a reasonable floor — if KNN found a good match, it should be visible), and that the arbiter verdict is rejected regardless. If either half is missing, the test doesn't prove what it claims to prove. A test that only checks the rejection without checking that similarity was high could pass even if KNN found no good match, which would mean the rejection happened for the wrong reason.
>
> The named-failures assertion for E51A's three thin cases is the one most likely to be skipped in practice and most important not to skip. Without it, the next round's first action after seeing 70% trace success would be to ask "which three cases?" and find the answer only by re-reading the evidence JSON. With the assertion, the answer is in the test output. More importantly, if a future change accidentally fixes one thin case while breaking a previously passing case, the named-failures list will catch it — the set of failures will be different from expected, even if the count is the same.
>
> **One additional assertion worth adding at the same time.**
>
> Assert that E51A's three thin cases are exactly those three and no others. The current framing is "assert they are recorded as named failures," which checks presence but not completeness. If the implementation records four failures instead of three — because a fourth case broke silently — the test would still pass. The assertion should be:
>
> ```
> Assert.Equal(
>     new[] { "V05-debug-log-removal", "V06-emoji-crash", "V08-call-sequence" },
>     e51aResult.NamedFailures.OrderBy(x => x).ToArray()
> );
> ```
>
> Exact set, not just "contains these." This means the thin cases are under version control in the test, not just in the evidence file.
>
> **The sequence for the next session.** Write these five tests first, run the full suite to confirm 890/890 passes (885 existing plus 5 new), and only then move to either the E51A data improvement work or the E51B scaling work. The hardening is one small session. The scaling is multiple sessions. Doing the hardening first means the scaling sessions will catch regressions automatically rather than discovering them through manual evidence review.
