> Good. I now have enough of the codebase to give a specific and useful answer.
>
> The findings from E51A and E51B apply to projects 21-23 in four distinct places, each with a different character.
>
> The RouteClassifier in project 22 has the same structural weakness E51A started with. It uses pure keyword scoring with no predicate profile input. E18 proved that predicate-based KNN adds roughly 12 percentage points over keyword matching on ambiguous prompts — exactly the compound-wording case that was V06's original failure. The RouteClassifier currently produces a confidence score from keyword count ratios, but it has no awareness of the logical structure underlying the request. The E51A finding says: compound diagnostic+repair prompts ("why and how to fix") will misroute at the keyword level because "why" and "how" pull toward CodeQuestion while "fix" and "crash" pull toward Bug. The fix for project 22 is the same fix that resolved V06 — add a training example cluster for compound wording, or feed the predicate profile from SemanticCompilerFacade into RouteClassifier alongside the keywords. The second option is cleaner because RouteClassifier already receives semanticTokens as its input, and the compiler pipeline is already integrated into the agent infrastructure through project 21.
>
> The KnnSkillFilter in project 22 has the domain-scoped retrieval gap that Phase 2 is about to address in E51A. The current implementation searches all skill candidates using semantic similarity without scoping to the classified domain first. E51A Phase 1 demonstrated that scoping KNN to the predicted domain pool before neighbor selection gives cleaner separation — V07's architecture case went from a single-point attractor to a genuine two-neighbor cluster once the pool was constrained. The KnnSkillFilter could apply the same pattern: after RouteClassifier classifies the domain, scope skillCandidates to skills tagged for that domain before calling _search.SearchAsync. This also adds the wrong-domain retrieval risk that Phase 2 is addressing — which means the guard test being written for E51A applies here too. If domain classification misroutes and the pool is wrong, the KNN will confidently return the best match from the wrong skill set. A confidence floor check on the filtered result, before returning it, would catch this.
>
> The three task decomposers in project 22 expose the same false-conjunction problem that E21 resolved, but at different levels of sophistication. ComplexTaskDecomposer uses conjunction-splitting without predicate awareness, which E21 showed produces wrong splits on prompts like "find methods that return null and log them." NgramTaskDecomposer improves this with a bigram boundary corpus. RoleBasedTaskDecomposer improves further with VERB+NOUN structural detection. The E51A finding adds one more layer: the predicate profile of the prompt, not just its surface structure, is the most reliable boundary signal. A prompt with two distinct predicate clusters (one NULL_GUARD-heavy on the left, one LOG_OP-heavy on the right) is genuinely split even if the VERB+NOUN rule would miss it. This is an enhancement to RoleBasedTaskDecomposer, not a replacement — add predicate-profile boundary weight alongside the existing role-tagging weight. The E51A evidence shows that predicate profiles are stable enough at 10 examples to use as a boundary signal, so the training data requirement is manageable.
>
> The AgentOrchestrator in project 22 and the AgentLoop in project 21 have no knowledge-edge detection. E51B proved that a small system can detect when it lacks the competence to answer a request — the biometric passport case created a context pack and learning gap packet instead of producing a confident wrong answer. Neither the orchestrator nor the agent loop currently has a mechanism for this. When RunAsync receives a task that the decomposer and context window cannot handle — because no relevant skills were retrieved and the code context is thin — the loop continues anyway, producing an answer from whatever partial context it assembled. The E51B design says this moment should produce a named gap signal, not a silent low-quality answer. Adding a confidence check on the assembled context — if selected.Count == 0 or usedTokens < threshold * tokenBudget, emit a knowledge-edge signal rather than running the LLM call — would be the project 21/22 equivalent of CH-01's context pack.
>
> The practical sequence for carrying these findings across. Start with the RouteClassifier improvement because it is the smallest and most direct transfer — it is one method in one class and the fix is validated by E51A's V06 evidence. Then add the domain-scoping improvement to KnnSkillFilter, which reuses the same pattern being built for E51A Phase 2 and means the guard test can be shared. The task decomposer predicate enhancement is a larger change and should wait until E51A Tier 2 produces more predicate boundary examples to draw training pairs from. The knowledge-edge detection in the agent loop is the most architectural and should follow after E51B scales to its next axis, since that scaling will produce the patterns that make the detection reliable.
>
> The existing tests for projects 21-23 are in the full suite that has been holding at 895/895. Any changes to those projects need to keep that number stable. The RouteClassifier fix is the one most likely to shift existing tests, since it changes classification behavior. Worth running the full suite specifically against project 22 tests after that change before touching anything else.

> Now I have the full picture. The existing infrastructure is more capable than it might appear from the outside — the approval pattern, idle learning, feedback routing, and LoRA training are all already present. The goal is to wire them together correctly around the internal-first principle. Let me lay out the design clearly.
>
> The cartoon you described — internal LLM does the work, external AI is asked only with explicit approval and a structured context pack, results feed back into local learning scheduled at idle time — maps almost exactly onto what projects 14, 16, 21, 22, and 23 already have as separate pieces. The work is connecting them, not building them from scratch.
>
> What already exists and is directly usable.
>
> The PermissionGate in project 21 already has the three-tier model: Allowed, RequiresApproval, Denied. Right now it applies to file-writing tools. The same pattern extends naturally to external API calls — add call_external_ai as a new tool name in the RequiresApproval set alongside edit_file and write_file. The approval path is already designed; it just does not yet cover the external AI case.
>
> The FeedbackRouter in project 14 already converts results into training signals: Accepted becomes a positive example, Edited becomes a DPO pair plus a positive example, Rejected becomes a negative DPO pair. The internal LLM's result examination — where the internal model judges its own output — maps directly onto the Edited and Accepted signals. The internal model examines the result, produces a corrected version if needed, and the feedback router stores both as a DPO pair.
>
> The AutonomousLearningPipeline in project 16 already has the idle-time gate: IdleDetector checks four conditions before any training runs. The IncrementalTrainer runs LoRA passes per domain. The ReplayBuffer (E43, D-06) prevents catastrophic forgetting. The pipeline exists; it just is not yet connected to the agent loop's output.
>
> The ILlmGateway in project 22 is the abstraction the ReactAgentLoop calls. Right now it is a single interface with one SendAsync method. The internal-first model means this interface should resolve to the internal LLM by default, and a separate IExternalAiGateway should be introduced for the external path — with the permission gate sitting between them.
>
> The five components to add, in the sequence they should be built.
>
> Component one: InternalLlmGateway. A concrete implementation of ILlmGateway that routes to the internal model from project 09 (the TextGenerator) and project 10 (LoRA adapter selection). The AgentPipeline and ReactAgentLoop already depend on ILlmGateway — swapping the concrete implementation is the change. The domain classifier from E51A determines which LoRA adapter loads for the current request before the call is made.
>
> Component two: ExternalAiRequestPackage. A record that captures exactly what E51B's context pack captures: the original request, the compiled logical structure, the internal model's attempt and its predicate profile, the confidence score, the specific missing competence statement (not "low confidence" — a named reason), the required answer shape, and the arbiter constraints that still apply. This is the structured prompt the user approves before any external call goes out. The PermissionGate check for call_external_ai returns this package to the caller, who displays it and waits for Allowed or Denied.
>
> Component three: ExternalAiResultAdapter. After the external call returns, this component runs the result through the same logical structure compiler that E51A and E51B use. It produces a FeedbackEvent with signal Edited — the external answer is the UserCorrection, the internal model's original attempt is the ModelResponse. This goes directly into FeedbackRouter.Route(), which stores the DPO pair and the positive example. No special-casing needed — the feedback infrastructure already handles exactly this shape.
>
> Component four: InternalResultExaminer. A second call to the internal LLM, after the primary response is produced, that asks the internal model to evaluate its own answer against the request's required predicate profile and arbiter constraints. This produces a structured examination result: which required predicates are present, which are absent, which arbiter constraints are satisfied, and an overall confidence score. If the examination score is above the confidence threshold, the result goes to FeedbackRouter as Accepted. If it is below, the result goes as Edited with the examiner's corrected version as the UserCorrection. The key architectural point: the examiner uses the same predicate vocabulary and arbiter rules that E51B established — it is not a free-form quality judgment but a structured check against named criteria.
>
> Component five: LearningEventScheduler. A thin coordinator that sits between the FeedbackRouter and the AutonomousLearningPipeline. When the feedback router accumulates more than a threshold of new DPO pairs for a domain (the threshold is configurable, starting at five pairs), it queues a learning event for that domain. The IdleDetector gates execution — the queue drains only when the four idle conditions are met. The IncrementalTrainer runs one LoRA pass per queued domain, the new adapter is registered, and the before/after accuracy comparison runs. If enhanced accuracy is lower than baseline, the adapter is rolled back, not installed.
>
> The flow from the user's perspective at runtime.
>
> The user gives a task. The agent classifies the domain, loads the matching LoRA adapter, assembles context through KnnSkillFilter scoped to the classified domain (the E51A Phase 2 finding), calls the internal LLM, receives a response. The InternalResultExaminer checks the response. If confident, the result is returned and logged as Accepted. If not confident, the examiner produces a correction and the result is returned with a note that the internal model flagged a gap — the user sees the best available internal answer.
>
> If the examiner identifies a specific missing competence — not just low confidence but a named gap like "the internal model has no examples of this error pattern" — the PermissionGate is invoked for call_external_ai. The user sees the ExternalAiRequestPackage: what the internal model attempted, what it couldn't handle, what the external call will ask, what format the answer must come back in, and which arbiter constraints still apply to whatever the external AI returns. The user approves or denies. If approved, the call goes out, the adapter runs the result through the ExternalAiResultAdapter, the DPO pair is stored, and the response is returned. If denied, the best internal answer is returned with the gap noted.
>
> At idle time, the LearningEventScheduler drains the queue. Domains with enough new DPO pairs get a LoRA training pass. Before/after accuracy is measured. Adapters that improve are installed; those that regress are kept as candidates but not promoted. The next request for that domain gets the improved adapter.
>
> What to add to projects 21-23 specifically, versus what stays in 14 and 16.
>
> Projects 14 and 16 own the learning infrastructure and should not change — they are the consumers of the DPO pairs and the training triggers. Projects 21-23 own the agent runtime and should gain: the InternalLlmGateway and ExternalAiRequestPackage in project 22's Fabric, the InternalResultExaminer in project 22's Pipeline, the call_external_ai entry in project 21's PermissionGate, and the LearningEventScheduler as a new component in project 21's Loop folder. Project 23 contributes the AgentStateMachine conditional edge that routes to the external-AI path when the examiner confidence drops below threshold — this is a new edge from the examine state to the approval-request state.
>
> The locked decision this adds. The internal LLM is always attempted first. External AI is only accessible through an explicit user-approved request package. Approval is scoped to one request — it does not grant persistent permission. All external AI results pass through the ExternalAiResultAdapter before entering the result path. All results, internal or external, are examined by the InternalResultExaminer before being returned. Accepted and corrected results are stored as training signals. Training runs at idle time only, gated by IdleDetector. This belongs in DECISIONS-LOCKED as D-14.
>
> The implementation sequence that respects the existing test baseline: add InternalLlmGateway first (it replaces no behavior, just makes the default concrete), then the InternalResultExaminer (additive), then the call_external_ai permission gate entry (additive), then the ExternalAiRequestPackage and adapter (additive), then the LearningEventScheduler (additive). Each step adds tests, and the full suite should hold at 897/897 or above throughout.

> Read role-based decomposer, codebase indexer, and file selector
> Good. I now have enough of the codebase to give a specific and useful answer.
>
> The findings from E51A and E51B apply to projects 21-23 in four distinct places, each with a different character.
>
> The RouteClassifier in project 22 has the same structural weakness E51A started with. It uses pure keyword scoring with no predicate profile input. E18 proved that predicate-based KNN adds roughly 12 percentage points over keyword matching on ambiguous prompts — exactly the compound-wording case that was V06's original failure. The RouteClassifier currently produces a confidence score from keyword count ratios, but it has no awareness of the logical structure underlying the request. The E51A finding says: compound diagnostic+repair prompts ("why and how to fix") will misroute at the keyword level because "why" and "how" pull toward CodeQuestion while "fix" and "crash" pull toward Bug. The fix for project 22 is the same fix that resolved V06 — add a training example cluster for compound wording, or feed the predicate profile from SemanticCompilerFacade into RouteClassifier alongside the keywords. The second option is cleaner because RouteClassifier already receives semanticTokens as its input, and the compiler pipeline is already integrated into the agent infrastructure through project 21.
>
> The KnnSkillFilter in project 22 has the domain-scoped retrieval gap that Phase 2 is about to address in E51A. The current implementation searches all skill candidates using semantic similarity without scoping to the classified domain first. E51A Phase 1 demonstrated that scoping KNN to the predicted domain pool before neighbor selection gives cleaner separation — V07's architecture case went from a single-point attractor to a genuine two-neighbor cluster once the pool was constrained. The KnnSkillFilter could apply the same pattern: after RouteClassifier classifies the domain, scope skillCandidates to skills tagged for that domain before calling _search.SearchAsync. This also adds the wrong-domain retrieval risk that Phase 2 is addressing — which means the guard test being written for E51A applies here too. If domain classification misroutes and the pool is wrong, the KNN will confidently return the best match from the wrong skill set. A confidence floor check on the filtered result, before returning it, would catch this.
>
> The three task decomposers in project 22 expose the same false-conjunction problem that E21 resolved, but at different levels of sophistication. ComplexTaskDecomposer uses conjunction-splitting without predicate awareness, which E21 showed produces wrong splits on prompts like "find methods that return null and log them." NgramTaskDecomposer improves this with a bigram boundary corpus. RoleBasedTaskDecomposer improves further with VERB+NOUN structural detection. The E51A finding adds one more layer: the predicate profile of the prompt, not just its surface structure, is the most reliable boundary signal. A prompt with two distinct predicate clusters (one NULL_GUARD-heavy on the left, one LOG_OP-heavy on the right) is genuinely split even if the VERB+NOUN rule would miss it. This is an enhancement to RoleBasedTaskDecomposer, not a replacement — add predicate-profile boundary weight alongside the existing role-tagging weight. The E51A evidence shows that predicate profiles are stable enough at 10 examples to use as a boundary signal, so the training data requirement is manageable.
>
> The AgentOrchestrator in project 22 and the AgentLoop in project 21 have no knowledge-edge detection. E51B proved that a small system can detect when it lacks the competence to answer a request — the biometric passport case created a context pack and learning gap packet instead of producing a confident wrong answer. Neither the orchestrator nor the agent loop currently has a mechanism for this. When RunAsync receives a task that the decomposer and context window cannot handle — because no relevant skills were retrieved and the code context is thin — the loop continues anyway, producing an answer from whatever partial context it assembled. The E51B design says this moment should produce a named gap signal, not a silent low-quality answer. Adding a confidence check on the assembled context — if selected.Count == 0 or usedTokens < threshold * tokenBudget, emit a knowledge-edge signal rather than running the LLM call — would be the project 21/22 equivalent of CH-01's context pack.
>
> The practical sequence for carrying these findings across. Start with the RouteClassifier improvement because it is the smallest and most direct transfer — it is one method in one class and the fix is validated by E51A's V06 evidence. Then add the domain-scoping improvement to KnnSkillFilter, which reuses the same pattern being built for E51A Phase 2 and means the guard test can be shared. The task decomposer predicate enhancement is a larger change and should wait until E51A Tier 2 produces more predicate boundary examples to draw training pairs from. The knowledge-edge detection in the agent loop is the most architectural and should follow after E51B scales to its next axis, since that scaling will produce the patterns that make the detection reliable.
>
> The existing tests for projects 21-23 are in the full suite that has been holding at 895/895. Any changes to those projects need to keep that number stable. The RouteClassifier fix is the one most likely to shift existing tests, since it changes classification behavior. Worth running the full suite specifically against project 22 tests after that change before touching anything else.

I think this is very good, and much closer to a usable “session discipline” document than a normal plan. It captures the real failure patterns, not abstract best practices.

The strongest parts:

- It correctly names the core failure: B describing the output instead of being the output.
- It preserves the “do not cut edges” lesson.
- It separates document-examination behavior, experiment behavior, and projects 21-23 runtime behavior.
- The E51/E52 evidence rules are concrete enough to test, not just “be careful.”
- The internal-first section is useful because it turns architecture into runtime guardrails.

I would fix a few things before treating it as canonical.

1. D-15 is now locked
The file says:

`D-15 (not yet locked, must be added)`

That is outdated. It should say D-15 is locked.

2. One paragraph contradicts itself
In “Do not let approval persist across loop iterations,” it says the guard returns false when `ApprovalRequestedKey` is true, then says two sequential checks in the same state must both return `RequiresApproval`.

Those are different layers:
- `PermissionGate.Check("call_external_ai")` returns `RequiresApproval`.
- `ExternalAiStateGuards.ShouldRequestExternalAiApproval(...)` returns false after approval was already requested.

This needs to be clarified.

3. “Do not use technical or code terms” is too absolute
For human-facing training pair prose, yes. But `node-00` compiler outputs, predicates, feature shapes, evidence JSON, and arbiter names must use formal terms. Better wording:

Use plain human language for natural-language A/B training content. Use canonical formal terms only where the node’s actual runtime output is formal structure.

4. “Dynamic-flow architecture plan is not source document” needs scope
That was true for the original Flow-01 task. But now we sometimes examine the architecture plan itself as a source document for adaptation. So I’d qualify it:

Do not treat the dynamic-flow architecture plan as the source document when the task is to translate gathered business/system documents into training sets.

5. Add the round-zip rule
Since you asked for round zips, this file should include a new general-session rule:

At the end of every completed round, create a zip containing changed/created files, manifest, verification, and session-start prompt.

Overall: yes, this is worth keeping. I’d make it `v2` with those corrections and then use it as the start-of-session guard document.

The E52 V06RoutingTrace uses it correctly — it calls InspectRouting, checks the domain and adapter path, and verifies ExternalCallCount is still zero. This pattern makes the gateway's routing logic independently testable without needing to mock an async call chain.

InspectRouting_BugDominantBoundary_LoadsBugAdapter testing "explain the fix pattern for avoiding null crashes in general" (CodeQ=1 explain, Bug=2 fix+null) and InspectRouting_QuestionDominantBoundary_LoadsCodeQuestionAdapter testing "what pattern should I use to avoid null crashes" (CodeQ=2 what+use, Bug=1 null) — these are exactly the near-miss cases that were flagged as the brittle boundary in the previous review. The behavior is now documented as locked expectations, not discovered in production.
>

This is more compact than the guidance's four separate tests but covers the same behavioral surface. > 982/982 with the rollback gate now enforced in the production pipeline. The implementation is correct on all dimensions worth checking.
>
> **The pipeline change is structurally right.** Steps 6 and 7 are now distinct. Step 6 builds the candidate adapter after training. Step 7 measures enhanced accuracy and compares it against baseline before calling `_registry.Register`. The gate is strict: `enhanced <= baseline` fails, not just `enhanced < baseline`. Equal accuracy is not an improvement — the candidate does not install. This prevents a degenerate case where the evaluator returns the same score twice (no learning occurred) from accidentally promoting a redundant adapter.
>
> **The `SequentialAccuracyAL` fake is the right design.** Using a `Queue<double>` seeded with `params double[] values` means the first `Evaluate` call returns the baseline score and the second returns the enhanced score — exactly mirroring what the production pipeline does at Step 2 and Step 7. The comment "validates that the pipeline measures accuracy both before and after training" makes the test's intent explicit. A fake that returned the same value from both calls would not prove sequencing; this one does.
>
> **The test assertions cover both the error path and the registry state.** Asserting `result.IsSuccess == false` proves the cycle failed. Asserting `result.ErrorCode == "ACCURACY_NOT_IMPROVED"` proves it failed for the right reason, not for some other early exit like `SYSTEM_ACTIVE` or `COLLECTION_FAILED`. Asserting `adapter.Value == null` proves the registry was not written — the candidate adapter does not exist in the registry after the failed cycle. Three assertions for one behavioral guarantee is the right level of coverage.
>
> **The `BuildPipelineWithRegistry` helper is a genuine addition.** The original tests used `BuildPipeline` which discarded the registry. This round added a variant that returns both the pipeline and the registry, making it possible to inspect registry state after a run. This will be useful for future tests that verify positive promotion (enhanced > baseline registers correctly) without needing to restructure the helper.
>
> **One thing to note for the next session.** The comment in Step 7 says "Same evaluator and test set as Step 2." The `SequentialAccuracyAL` fake enforces this by sequencing the calls, but in production the `IAccuracyEvaluator` implementation will need to use the same evaluation criteria for both calls — otherwise baseline and enhanced are not comparable. This is a documentation note for the production evaluator implementation, not a test gap. The test correctly proves the gate logic; the production evaluator is responsible for measurement consistency.

I checked the external batches against the continuation plan. Short version: **do not add these directly to the local learning sets yet.** They are useful candidate material, but they are not final learning-set batches under the method.

**Main Findings**

1. **Wrong final shape.**
The plan requires final node learning files with `Pair [ID]`, full `A`, full `B`, `Reason`, and a rephrased companion pair. See [EXAMINATION-CONTINUATION-PLAN-v1.0.md](<./plan the learning set/EXAMINATION-CONTINUATION-PLAN-v1.0.md:2141>).
The batch folder has **0** `Pair [...]` entries and **0** `Phrasing B` entries. These are structured candidate rows, not final node training pairs.

2. **No rephrasing layer.**
The plan requires every pair to appear with at least one rephrasing. The parsed rows have no rephrase fields, and the folder search found no rephrasing-pair format. This blocks promotion.

3. **Machine ingestion is not clean.**
There are **74 batch files**, **1,480 row IDs**, and no duplicate row IDs, which is good. But only **1,304 fenced JSON blocks** exist; **106 JSON blocks fail parsing**, mostly because large markdown/code outputs are placed inside JSON strings without proper escaping. Example: [ext-batch-061-090.md](<./external-sources/batches/ext-batch-061-090.md:770>).
Also, several files are markdown-field format, not JSON at all, for example [ext-batch-1621-1650.md](<./external-sources/batches/ext-batch-1621-1650.md:1>).

4. **Batch naming is misleading.**
Every file name implies 30 rows, but each file contains 20 row records. Example: [ext-batch-001-030.md](<./external-sources/batches/ext-batch-001-030.md:1>) says `EXT-001 through EXT-030`, but the file has 20 rows. Later examples are more confusing: `ext-batch-1021-1050.md` starts with `EXT-691 through EXT-710`.

5. **License gate is not strict enough.**
The plan says exact source-unit license must be confirmed before writing pairs, and unknown license means no pairs. See [EXAMINATION-CONTINUATION-PLAN-v1.0.md](<./plan the learning set/EXAMINATION-CONTINUATION-PLAN-v1.0.md:238>).
But the batches contain many vague license values: **296 `attribution`**, **104 `notice`**, plus IETF/CWE/MITRE variants requiring policy decisions. Some rows marked `approved` still only say `attribution`, e.g. [ext-batch-2161-2190.md](<./external-sources/batches/ext-batch-2161-2190.md:41>).
There are also GPL source rows, e.g. [ext-batch-271-300.md](<./external-sources/batches/ext-batch-271-300.md:48>), which should not move forward unless explicitly reclassified or excluded.

6. **Identifier/provenance drift.**
Row IDs and source IDs use several incompatible shapes:
`EXT-SEC-001`, `EXT-437-R1`, `ROW-EXT531-F1-A`, `EXT-691-A1`, `EXT-1451`.
Source IDs sometimes point to registry names, e.g. [ext-batch-001-030.md](<./external-sources/batches/ext-batch-001-030.md:35>), and sometimes to ledger units, e.g. [ext-batch-631-660.md](<./external-sources/batches/ext-batch-631-660.md:237>). This needs normalization before local learning import.

**What Is Usable**

The content itself is valuable. Many rows have real runtime-shaped input, concrete accepted/rejected outputs, arbiters, reasons, and source anchors. So these are a strong **candidate pool**.

**What Must Happen Before Import**

Normalize them into one canonical row schema, repair invalid JSON or convert all rows to JSONL, apply a hard license gate, split rows into node-specific learning-set files, write real `A→B` pairs plus rephrasing pairs, and add the required `00-INDEX.md`, `01-UML-FRAME.md`, `COVERAGE-LEDGER.jsonl`, and `10-SIMULATION-CHECK.md`.

My recommendation: treat the current folder as **preprocessed candidate material**, not learning-set material. The next useful step is a cleanup/conversion pass that produces a small clean promotion batch first, maybe 20 to 40 rows with clean MIT/Apache/CC-BY/public-domain licenses only.

> what about producing a zip on each round?

Yes. For this work, **a zip per round should be mandatory**.

A round is not closed until it produces:

1. `00-ROUND-MANIFEST.md`
   What this round tried to do, what changed, what is still blocked.

2. `01-FILES-INCLUDED.md`
   Exact list of produced/changed files, with relative paths.

3. `02-VALIDATION-RESULTS.md`
   Counts, parsing results, license-gate result, failures, blocked rows.

4. `03-NEXT-ROUND-PROMPT.md`
   Fixed session-start prompt for the next executor.

5. `files/`
   The actual changed or produced files, preserving folder structure.

6. `evidence/`
   Scripts, reports, JSON summaries, parse outputs, simulation checks.

For these external batches, the zip rule should be:

**No promotion zip, no import into local learning sets.**

Suggested naming:

```text
external-learning-round-001-inventory-and-gate.zip
external-learning-round-002-schema-normalization.zip
external-learning-round-003-license-clean-promotion-set.zip
external-learning-round-004-node-pair-conversion.zip
```

And the hard close rule:

```text
A round zip is valid only if the manifest says:
- what files were examined
- what files were produced or changed
- which rows are accepted, held, blocked, or malformed
- which plan checks passed or failed
- what the next round must do
```

For the current check, the next round zip should probably be:

```text
external-learning-round-001-batch-audit.zip
```

Its purpose: preserve the audit result before anyone starts fixing or converting the rows.

Node-02 is a language model unit that receives one domain packet and generates the full translated domain statement including the handoff marker as part of its output. The marker is not added by a router or a rules engine — it is part of what node-02 learns to produce.
> This is worth thinking through carefully because it has an implication for the training pairs.
> The markers are string values in the B output. The model learns to produce the right marker by seeing the pattern across training pairs: a covered packet always produces ready_for_scheme_planner, a boundary packet always produces send_to_scheme_planner_with_boundary_flag, and so on. The model learns the association between coverage_status in the A input and handoff_marker in the B output. After enough examples it should generalize — a new covered packet it has never seen before should produce ready_for_scheme_planner, and a new knowledge-edge packet should produce route_to_knowledge_edge_context_pack.
> The implication for node-03 is that the A inputs for scheme planner pairs should include the handoff markers as the model actually received them, because that is what node-02 will produce at runtime. The planner is not receiving hand-crafted clean inputs — it is receiving whatever node-02 generated, markers included. If the training pairs for node-03 show clean formal statements without markers, the planner is being trained on a different input shape than it will actually see.
> There is a second implication worth naming. Because the markers are model output rather than deterministic rule output, they can be wrong. A model trained on a small set might produce ready_for_scheme_planner on a boundary packet if the boundary case is underrepresented. This is why the arbiter units (node-08) exist downstream — they catch cases where the translator or planner produced something that should not have passed. The arbiter is not a redundant check on clean work; it is the safety net for the cases where earlier nodes misjudged their coverage.
> This also means the boundary markers, conflict markers, and knowledge-edge markers in the node-02 B outputs are not just documentation — they are the primary signal the scheme planner uses to decide whether to plan normally, plan with a gap flag, route to an external help request, or reject the downstream work. > Claude responded: Good question to ask now.
> Good question to ask now. Let me be direct about where the gap actually is.
>
> The training set work is not a prerequisite for testing the dynamic flow end to end. It is a prerequisite for training the LLM nodes to handle novel inputs well. Those are different things.
>
> What is needed for an actual end-to-end test of the dynamic flow architecture is not a complete training corpus — it is wired nodes that can execute the pipeline on a fixed known input. The E51B experiment already proved the flow works for six specific traces using the 12 teaching records. That was a closed-loop proof, not a full pipeline execution.
>
> A real end-to-end test of the full 9-node pipeline needs four things, and the training sets are only one of them.
>
> The first thing is the node implementations. Each node needs to be a running C# service that accepts the defined input shape and produces the defined output shape. Right now the nodes exist as training pair definitions and architecture documents. They do not exist as deployed C# code. The InternalLlmGateway, the domain classifier, the predicate extractor — these are implemented in projects 21-23. But the full 9-node pipeline as a connected sequence of services is not yet assembled.
>
> The second thing is the routing infrastructure. The dynamic flow topology lives in a database. The orchestrator reads the topology at runtime and routes each unit's output to the next node. This infrastructure exists in the architecture design but the actual C# orchestrator that reads the topology and dispatches work has not been built yet.
>
> The third thing is enough training data to make the LLM nodes respond usefully on a test input. For a closed end-to-end test on one fixed scenario, this does not need to be the full corpus. It needs enough pairs that node-00 through node-09 each produce a recognizable output for that one scenario. The E51B 12-teaching-record experiment proved this works at minimum scale for the registration domain. So three or four pairs per node, on one scenario, is enough to run a meaningful closed test.
>
> The fourth thing is a test harness. A way to inject a known prompt, trace the output through all nine nodes, and assert that each node's output matches the expected shape.
>
> So the honest answer is: the training set work will not end before you can test. You can test with what you have now for the registration domain, because E51B already validated the minimum viable training set for that scenario. > Claude responded: That reframes the entire project scope.
> That reframes the entire project scope. Let me absorb what you are saying before responding.
>
> The dynamic flow is not primarily a code-generation pipeline. It is an orchestration architecture — a way of managing complex multi-step problems through a structured sequence of decomposition, planning, processing, review, and formatting. The LLM nodes are the decision-making units. The stack they happen to produce output about is irrelevant to whether the orchestration itself works.
>
> What you actually want to prove is three things.
>
> First, can the flow correctly decompose a genuinely complex problem into the right domain territories, plan the right sub-tasks in the right order, process each sub-task completely, and produce a coherent result — without losing track of dependencies, constraints, or conflicting requirements along the way.
>
> Second, can the arbiters catch the cases where earlier nodes made wrong judgments — not just flag pre-identified bad patterns, but actually notice when a plan is incomplete, when a result contradicts a constraint, or when a domain was missed in the split.
>
> Third, does the architecture hold at problem complexity that no single LLM call handles well — the cases where the problem crosses four or five domains, has parallel paths, has wait states, and has review requirements that depend on earlier results.
>
> If those three things hold, the stack is irrelevant. The same orchestrator handles a Django N+1 problem, a multi-tenant authorization design, a data migration with zero-downtime requirements, or a registration flow with biometric proofing — because the decomposition, planning, and review logic is domain-agnostic. The domain translator is the only node that speaks domain vocabulary. Everything else operates on structure.
>
> This means the right test is not "does node-02 produce the correct formal description of a Django queryset problem." The right test is: give the flow a problem that is genuinely hard to orchestrate — one with conflicting requirements, multiple domains, a knowledge edge, and at least one case where a naive plan would produce something that violates a constraint — and see whether the flow catches the violation, handles the knowledge edge correctly, and produces a coherent result despite the complexity.
>
> The training set work as currently structured is optimizing for the wrong thing. It is teaching nodes to produce correct outputs for clean known scenarios. That proves the nodes work. It does not prove the orchestration works under pressure.
>
> What would prove the orchestration works is running the full pipeline on three or four genuinely hard multi-domain scenarios — problems where the right answer requires the planner to see that two domain paths have a dependency, the arbiters to catch that a proposed result violates a constraint introduced in a different domain, and the knowledge-edge path to fire correctly when a domain is outside the training set. The training data for this does not need to be comprehensive. It needs to be honest about what the system knows and does not know, and the arbiters need to be strong enough to catch the cases where nodes overstep.
>
> The stack independence question is a direct consequence of this. If the orchestration logic is correct, the same flow produces the right orchestration whether the downstream action is C# code, a Kubernetes manifest, a database migration plan, or a written explanation for a product manager. The formatter is the only node that touches the output shape. The planner, processor, and arbiters operate on the problem structure, not the output format.
>
> So the concrete recommendation is to stop the node-by-node training set work for now and run a real orchestration test on one hard scenario. Pick a problem that is genuinely complex — something with four or five domain territories, at least one constraint that a naive plan would violate, at least one knowledge edge, and at least one case where two sub-tasks have a real dependency that must be preserved. Run the full pipeline manually, using the existing training pairs where nodes are trained and human judgment where they are not yet trained. Record where the orchestration holds and where it breaks. That is the real signal.

> **The scenario selection is correct.** The complex onboarding migration scenario was already validated by E51B, which means the ground truth is known. The orchestrator is not being tested against an invented scenario — it is being tested against a scenario where the correct outputs at every node are already established. This is the right starting point because any failure at a node boundary can be unambiguously classified as orchestration failure versus training gap failure. The scenario also contains every orchestration pressure point: sequential dependencies, a genuine conflict (the duplicate account request), a knowledge edge (biometric passport), a boundary (resume state), and a no-stack constraint. One scenario, eight ability types under test simultaneously.
>
> **The deterministic fixture approach is the correct design decision.** The plan makes the reasoning explicit: live LLM variance would blur whether a failure came from orchestration or model wording. Running with deterministic station outputs first isolates the orchestration logic from model quality. After the deterministic proof passes, stations are replaced with learned units one at a time. Each replacement run produces a before/after comparison against the same evidence schema. This is exactly the right experimental methodology — it gives a clean signal at each step.
>
> **The eight metrics with specific quantitative targets are what elevate this from a narrative plan to a testable experiment.** `lost_edge_count = 0`, `dependency_violation_count = 0`, `duplicate_creation_accepted = false`, `invented_biometric_plan_items = 0`, `forbidden_stack_term_count = 0`, `human_result_sections_present = 5/5`. Every one of these is checkable from the evidence JSON without human interpretation. The evidence schema mandates three output formats — JSON for machine verification, markdown for human readability, Mermaid for topology visualization — which means the experiment is self-documenting.
>
> **The failure classification section at the end is the most valuable part of the plan.** It converts a binary pass/fail experiment into a diagnostic instrument. If edges are lost, the priority is edge preservation and trace schema. If dependencies are wrong, the priority is node-03 planner training. If arbiters do not block the duplicate account, the priority is arbiter selector and units. If the human result is unreadable, the priority is nodes 06 and 09. This is why the plan correctly says E53 should happen before more broad pair-writing — it tells us which training sets matter rather than treating all nodes as equally important.
>
> **One observation about the execution sequence.** Round A produces six documents before any code. The expected trace document is the critical one — it is the oracle that all ten test gates check against. The executor writing the expected trace needs to know the correct output at every node boundary for the onboarding scenario. The node-00 through node-02 outputs can be derived mechanically from the accepted training pairs. The node-03 scheme plan is the first document in the expected trace that requires genuine orchestration judgment — it must show the dependency ordering correctly, name the parallel groups, and preserve the boundary and knowledge-edge paths. If the expected trace gets the node-03 plan wrong, the tests will certify incorrect orchestration. The review gate after Round A should pay particular attention to whether the expected trace's node-03 plan correctly sequences provider trust before account resolution, account resolution before questionnaire continuation, and policy acceptance before full activation.

> The guidance is organized around the three actions that every passing experiment produces, in a fixed order that must not be skipped.
>
> Why the order matters. Action 1 (corrections) must finish before action 2 (gap closure) because gap closure pairs are written in the examination domain vocabulary, and that vocabulary assumes the source pairs it references are correct. If a gap closure pair for node-08 teaches the arbiter to detect an applier crossover, and the CB1-03-002 pair still contains the uncorrected crossover text, the node-08 pair is teaching detection of something that will be corrected away. The training signal becomes inconsistent.
>
> The pair count rule in action 2. One original plus one phrasing B per scenario per node that needs a new pair. Not twenty pairs per experiment — eight for a three-scenario experiment with four nodes requiring new pairs. The pass gates from the experiment are the evidence that the minimum is sufficient. Adding more pairs before validating the minimum means the minimum was never tested.
>
> The B shape for each node is non-negotiable. The guidance includes the exact shapes because the most common failure in pair writing is a B that describes what the output should contain rather than containing it. For node-08 specifically: the pass case is silence or just the word "pass." No explanation. No acknowledgment. The trained arbiter must learn that a correct result produces nothing — not a paragraph explaining why no concern was raised. CB2-07-002 correctly demonstrates this and the node-08 pairs for the examination domain must follow the same pattern.

>
> Let me work through what is actually ready and what is not.
>
> What the current orchestration proves.
>
> E53 proves the nine-node pipeline correctly manages one complex problem end to end — decomposing it into domain territories, planning with real dependencies, handling knowledge edges, rejecting conflicts, and producing honest human-readable output. The architecture is stack-independent and domain-agnostic by design. The pipeline does not care whether the input is a user registration problem, a Django N+1 fix, or a UI/UX definition task. What it cares about is whether the logical structure compiler can extract meaning, whether the domain splitter can identify the relevant territories, and whether the scheme planner can produce a correctly ordered plan with real dependencies.
>
> That generalization is already proven at the architectural level. The problem is the training corpus, not the architecture.
>
> Where the current corpus is bounded.
>
> The training pairs that exist today teach the nodes to recognize registration domain vocabulary, infrastructure orchestration vocabulary (OTel, EF Core, Dapper, Redis, Karpenter), and the examination vocabulary produced by the five experiments. When you give the pipeline a UI/UX definition task, node-01 will try to split it into domain packets using the signal rules it has learned. If none of those signals match the UI/UX vocabulary — wireframe fidelity, accessibility compliance, design system token consistency, interaction model — the splitter will either produce the wrong packets or fall back to the registration domain's signal rules and produce irrelevant packets.
>
> The same problem cascades through every downstream node. Node-02 cannot produce formal domain statements in UI/UX vocabulary if it has never seen that vocabulary. Node-03 cannot produce a correctly ordered plan for a UI/UX definition phase if it has never seen what the dependencies between design decisions look like. The arbiters cannot catch a missing accessibility review if they have never been trained to recognize that as a domain responsibility.
>
> What extending to new phases and sub-phases requires.
>
> Each major phase area you named — UI/UX definition, functional specs, technical design, implementation, testing, QA, QA automation — is a new domain family. Each domain family requires its own set of training pairs across the relevant nodes. The good news is that the experiment method scales directly. You have the translation method, the experiment design method, and the learning set structure method. Each new phase area follows the same process: identify the source documents that govern that phase, translate them into experiments using the six-step method, run the experiments to validate the pairs, and close the gaps.
>
> The bad news is that this is a significant corpus expansion. A rough count: if each phase area has four to six sub-domains (UI/UX alone has layout, interaction, accessibility, design system, motion, responsiveness), and each sub-domain needs pairs across six to eight nodes, you are looking at several hundred pairs per phase area before the orchestrator can handle that area without falling back to human proxy.
>
> What makes continuous extension genuinely hard.
>
> The architecture supports it. The experiment method supports it. The learning set method supports it. What does not yet exist is the cross-phase dependency management.
>
> Consider the transition from technical design to implementation. A technical design decision — "this component uses an event-driven architecture with a command bus" — creates a constraint that the implementation phase inherits. The implementation orchestrator must know about this constraint without re-reading the entire technical design document. In E53, the constraints come from the source packet. In a multi-phase system, the constraints come from upstream phase outputs.
>
> This is a pipeline-of-pipelines problem. The nine-node pipeline handles one phase of work. For continuous extension across phases and sub-phases, you need a mechanism that takes the output of the UI/UX phase orchestration and makes it available as structured input to the functional spec phase orchestration, and so on down the chain. The current architecture does not have this mechanism yet. The source packet for each run is currently hand-authored. For true cross-phase continuity, the source packet for each downstream phase must be derived from the outputs of upstream phases, with constraints, decisions, and knowledge edges preserved across phase boundaries.
>
> What is ready to start now.
>
> Three things can happen in parallel without waiting for the cross-phase mechanism.
>
> First, each phase area can be orchestrated independently. The UI/UX definition phase orchestrator can run as a standalone pipeline that takes a design brief as its source packet and produces an orchestration plan, identified knowledge edges, and rejected design decisions. This is exactly what E53 does for the onboarding scenario. It does not yet connect to the functional spec phase, but it proves the orchestration works for that domain.
>
> Second, the training corpus can be extended domain by domain. Pick one phase area — technical design is the right first choice because it has the most overlap with the infrastructure orchestration vocabulary already in the corpus — and run it through the translation and experiment process. The pairs produced become the foundation for that phase area's orchestrator.
>
> Third, the cross-phase mechanism can be designed in parallel with the domain expansion. The mechanism is fundamentally a structured handoff protocol — the output of one phase orchestration becomes the source packet for the next, with constraints, decisions, knowledge edges, and learning gap packets carried forward. This is the same pattern as the learning gap packets in E53, extended across phase boundaries rather than within a single run.
>
> The concrete recommendation.
>
> Start with one complete phase area end to end before trying to connect phases. Technical design is the right choice because it sits at the center of your dependency chain — it receives inputs from functional specs and produces outputs for implementation. Proving that the orchestrator handles technical design correctly, with the right domain vocabulary, the right dependency ordering, and the right knowledge edge handling, establishes the pattern for every other phase area. The cross-phase mechanism can then be designed against a concrete example of what phase output looks like rather than against an abstract specification.
>
> The scaling problem is a corpus problem, not an architecture problem. The architecture already generalizes. The corpus needs to catch up to it one phase area at a time.
>

> The guide is organized to be usable as a working reference, not just a description.
>
> On the phase and sub-phase structure. Seven phases, twenty-seven sub-phases. Each sub-phase has a single question it must answer before it is complete — that question is the clearest signal for whether a document belongs there. A document that answers "what token values are non-negotiable across all screens" belongs to sub-phase 1.1 regardless of what it is titled or where it is filed. The question-it-answers formulation is more reliable than any other classification signal because it forces you to think about what problem the document resolves rather than what topic it covers.
>
> On the document identification method. Two questions in sequence, four clarifying rules, and two readiness checks. The two questions — what problem does the document resolve, and what vocabulary does it use — are enough to place most documents correctly. The vocabulary list maps domain terms to sub-phase assignments without requiring judgment about the content. The four rules handle the common edge cases: a session plan that references Phase 3 decisions belongs to Phase 4, not Phase 3. A document with only vague statements is not ready to be an experiment source.
>
> The most important rule is Rule 4 — absence is a signal. When a sub-phase has no document, that sub-phase is a knowledge edge in the orchestration. The correct response is to name it as missing and mark the sub-phase as boundary, exactly as the biometric passport verification knowledge edge was handled in E53. This prevents the orchestrator from inventing content for a sub-phase that has no source authority.

It exists as a **proved experiment**, not yet as a functional assistant unit.

The important nuance: pieces of the assistant exist in production-adjacent projects, but the actual dynamic-flow “orchestrator assistant” is still encoded as experiments and evidence.

**Current State**

- `35.ExperimentsV2` proves the architecture:
  - E53 proves the 9-node orchestration path.
  - T34 proves Phase 3 -> Phase 4 transition logic.
  - Evidence is JSON/Markdown/Mermaid.
  - Tests assert packet counts, edge preservation, concerns/blocks/pass, human result quality.

- Projects `21`, `22`, `23` contain useful runtime pieces:
  - internal-first LLM gateway
  - external AI approval guard
  - feedback routing hooks
  - learning scheduler
  - route classifier
  - KNN skill filter
  - state machine guards

- Project `15.OrchestratorModel` has a simpler orchestrator facade:
  - classify -> decompose -> sort -> launch -> merge -> quality check -> memory
  - but it is not the predicate-level dynamic-flow machine.

So: **the intelligence has been proven, but it is not yet exposed as a reusable runtime service.**

**What Is Required**

To make it functional, we need a real unit like:

`IDynamicFlowOrchestrator` / `IOrchestratorAssistant`

with one public operation:

```csharp
RunAsync(request, sourceDocuments, options, ct)
```

and it must perform the real flow:

1. Compile input into 22-predicate logical structure.
2. Route through phase/sub-phase/domain topology.
3. Execute dynamic-flow stations as runtime units, not experiment fixtures.
4. Preserve trace evidence at every edge.
5. Apply arbiters.
6. Produce human-readable result.
7. Emit learning gaps and feedback events.
8. Store evidence/context for later learning.

**The Missing Functional Pieces**

1. **Runtime service wrapper**
   A production `OrchestratorAssistantService` with a stable API.

2. **Topology runner**
   Something that reads a flow topology and executes nodes, array nodes, gates, and transitions.

3. **Runtime node interface**
   One common unit contract for node-00 through node-09 and future phase tools.

4. **Storage layer**
   Flow registry, unit registry, dataset registry, decision graph, context packet store, event log.

5. **Experiment-to-runtime adapter**
   The E53/T34 proof logic must be converted from deterministic experiment classes into reusable runtime station implementations.

6. **Assistant API/CLI entry point**
   A way for a user or app to call it with documents and a task.

7. **Learning loop integration**
   Feedback and failed transitions must feed local learning sets and idle training.

**Shortest path**

Build the functional unit around T34/E53 first:

- `OrchestratorAssistantService`
- in-memory topology registry
- in-memory evidence store
- deterministic E53/T34 station adapters
- one API/CLI call that returns final human result + evidence path

Then replace deterministic stations with trained/internal units one by one.

That gives you a real assistant early, while keeping the experiment gates as protection.

> Reading the codebase and the plan before assessing.Now I have everything I need. I have read the full T34 proof, the test structure, the OperationResult envelope, the project layout, and the plan document. Writing the assessment.
>
> ---
>
> The plan is structurally sound and the phasing discipline is correct. The assessment below covers what is right, what needs precision before Phase 25 starts, and one design decision the plan leaves open that needs to be resolved now.
>
> **What the plan gets right.**
>
> The one-unit-presence-per-phase rule is the most important constraint in the plan and it is correctly enforced. Every phase change table follows it. The T35 replacement proof is designed correctly — T34 stays as oracle, T35 creates the same input, calls the new unit for node-01 only, and compares output against the oracle. This is the right shape for proving a unit replacement without drifting metrics.
>
> The flag taxonomy is well-structured. Separating optimization flags (default true, may be disabled in ablation experiments) from safety flags (must be true in product paths, may only be disabled in negative-control proofs) from experiment control flags (describe how a proof runs, not product behavior) is the right three-way split. The `UseArbiterAuthority` and `UseKnowledgeEdgeDetection` flags correctly cannot be turned off without explicitly acknowledging you are running a negative-control experiment.
>
> The target contract shape is correct. `ILogicalUnit<TInput, TOutput>` returning `OperationResult<LogicalUnitResult<TOutput>>` is consistent with the existing envelope pattern in `AgentInfrastructure.Core`. The synchronous-first decision is correct — the first replacement is deterministic, and adding async before a single trained unit exists creates complexity with no benefit.
>
> **What needs precision before Phase 25 starts.**
>
> Three things in the plan are described at the right level of intent but need one more decision each before an executor can write the first file.
>
> First, the `LogicalContracts.cs` file path is given as `35.ExperimentsV2\LogicalFlow\LogicalContracts.cs`. The `LogicalFlow` folder does not exist yet. The executor needs to know: create it as a subfolder under `35.ExperimentsV2`, not as a new project. The plan implies this but does not state it. One line in the Phase 25 section: "create the `LogicalFlow` subfolder inside `35.ExperimentsV2`" removes any ambiguity.
>
> Second, the `LogicalExecutionFlags` record is listed as a parameter in the Phase 25 contract shape but its fields are shown as `(...)`. The executor needs the actual field list before writing the file, because the Phase 26 test that proves default flags are enabled must enumerate specific properties. The plan document contains the full flag taxonomy. The record needs one bool property per flag, with `init` setters and the correct defaults. The exact shape matters because Phase 26 tests call `Assert.True(flags.UseCompiledPredicateRepresentation)` — that property name must match the record definition.
>
> Third, `LogicalUnitMetadata` is declared in the contract shape but not used by `ILogicalUnit`. Its purpose needs to be stated before the file is written so the executor does not invent a use. The plan should either use it in the interface signature — for example, as a property on `LogicalUnitResult` — or remove it from Phase 25 and introduce it in a later phase when its purpose is clear.
>
> **The one design decision the plan leaves open.**
>
> The `ILogicalUnit` interface signature in the plan is:
>
> ```csharp
> OperationResult<LogicalUnitResult<TOutput>> Execute(LogicalUnitRequest<TInput> request);
> ```
>
> This is synchronous. The plan notes that async is introduced when a production LLM-backed unit is added. That is correct. But the plan does not say how the interface will become async without breaking every caller that implemented the synchronous version. There are two options and they have different consequences:
>
> Option A — introduce a separate `IAsyncLogicalUnit<TInput, TOutput>` interface alongside the synchronous one. Callers that need async implement the async interface. Callers that are deterministic implement the synchronous one. The orchestrator can hold references to both. This keeps the synchronous path untouched but doubles the interface surface.
>
> Option B — make the interface async from the start, returning `Task<OperationResult<LogicalUnitResult<TOutput>>>`. Synchronous implementations wrap their result in `Task.FromResult`. This is one more line per deterministic unit but the orchestrator only needs one interface type. This is the more common .NET pattern and avoids the interface proliferation of Option A.
>
> The plan should pick one before Phase 25, because the test for the flag defaults in Phase 25 will exercise the interface, and whichever shape is chosen in Phase 25 becomes the contract that Phase 26 must match.
>
> The recommendation is Option B — async from the start with `Task.FromResult` in deterministic units. The overhead is one line per deterministic unit, the benefit is a single interface that does not need to be replaced when the first trained unit arrives.
>
> **The T35 acceptance criteria need one addition.**
>
> The current T35 machine gates list seven metrics. They are correct. One gate is missing that becomes important the moment a real unit replaces a deterministic fixture: the confidence score gate. The T34 oracle produces node-01 packets with deterministic coverage statuses. When a real unit produces those packets, it also emits a confidence score through `LogicalUnitResult.Confidence`. The T35 gates should include:
>
> ```
> unit_min_confidence >= 0.70
> ```
>
> This is the wrong-domain retrieval guard from E51A — all wrong-domain neighbors came in below 0.50, and 0.70 was the correct-domain floor. Adding this gate now means T35 will fail gracefully if the first real unit's confidence is too low, rather than passing on metric parity while hiding a confidence collapse.
>
> **Summary for the executor.**
>
> Phase 25 is ready to start with three precise changes to the plan: state explicitly that `LogicalFlow` is a subfolder inside `35.ExperimentsV2`, expand `LogicalExecutionFlags` to list all thirteen flag properties with their defaults and `init` setters, and either use `LogicalUnitMetadata` in the interface or remove it from Phase 25. Resolve the sync/async question before writing the first file — Option B (async with `Task.FromResult` in deterministic units) is recommended. Add the `unit_min_confidence >= 0.70` gate to the T35 acceptance criteria.
>
> Everything else in the plan is correct and can proceed as written.

Yes. The current `LogicalOrchestratorAssistant` can become the proper `ILogicalOrchestrator`, but not by stuffing all behavior into that class. Right now it is a thin wrapper over one hardcoded T34 flow. To make it capable of adding/editing domains, phases, sub-phases, and transitions, it needs to become the command router over a mutable logical topology registry.

**Current State**
[LogicalOrchestratorAssistant.cs](C:/Projects/llm_mvp_core/15.OrchestratorModel/Logical/LogicalOrchestratorAssistant.cs) currently does three things:

1. Registers only T34 in memory.
2. Builds a `LogicalOrchestratorRequest`.
3. Delegates to `ILogicalOrchestrator`.

So it is assistant-shaped, but not yet a real topology-management orchestrator.

**What Needs To Change**

The assistant should route two classes of request:

1. **Run a flow**
   “Execute the technical-design to implementation transition.”

2. **Mutate the flow topology**
   “Add a QA automation phase after QA.”
   “Edit the testing sub-phase to include regression risk review.”
   “Add a transition rule from technical design to implementation.”

That means we need one new logical flow:

`TopologyMutationFlow : ILogicalFlow<LogicalTopologyCommand>`

This flow would contain units like:

- `TopologyIntentClassifierUnit`
- `DomainMutationPlannerUnit`
- `PhaseMutationPlannerUnit`
- `SubPhaseMutationPlannerUnit`
- `TransitionMutationPlannerUnit`
- `TopologyArbiterUnit`
- `TopologyApplyUnit`
- `TopologyEvidenceFormatterUnit`

**Required Data Structures**

A minimal command shape:

```csharp
public sealed record LogicalTopologyCommand(
    string Operation,       // add_domain, edit_phase, add_transition, etc.
    string TargetType,      // domain, phase, sub_phase, transition
    string TargetId,
    string UserRequest,
    IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object> Patch,
    string Reason);
```

A minimal topology model:

```csharp
public sealed record LogicalDomain(string Id, string Name, string Description);
public sealed record LogicalPhase(string Id, string DomainId, string Name, int Order);
public sealed record LogicalSubPhase(string Id, string PhaseId, string Name, int Order);
public sealed record LogicalTransition(string Id, string FromId, string ToId, string Rule, string[] RequiredPredicates);
```

And a registry:

```csharp
public interface ILogicalTopologyRegistry
{
    OperationResult<LogicalDomain> AddOrUpdateDomain(LogicalDomain domain);
    OperationResult<LogicalPhase> AddOrUpdatePhase(LogicalPhase phase);
    OperationResult<LogicalSubPhase> AddOrUpdateSubPhase(LogicalSubPhase subPhase);
    OperationResult<LogicalTransition> AddOrUpdateTransition(LogicalTransition transition);
}
```

**Where It Belongs**

The biggest correction: `ILogicalUnit`, `ILogicalFlow`, and `ILogicalOrchestrator` should not live only in `35.ExperimentsV2`.

They should move to a runtime-safe place, likely:

`C:/Projects/llm_mvp_core/21.AgentInfrastructure/Logical`

Then:

- project 21 owns the shared logical contracts
- project 22 implements logical units
- project 23 can adapt state-machine nodes into logical units
- project 15 hosts the assistant-facing orchestrator
- project 35 remains experiment proof, not runtime dependency owner

**How `LogicalOrchestratorAssistant` Evolves**

Current:

```csharp
CreateDefault() -> register T34 only -> run scenario
```

Future:

```csharp
RunAsync(userRequest)
    -> classify request as RunFlow or MutateTopology
    -> if RunFlow: resolve matching ILogicalFlow
    -> if MutateTopology: run TopologyMutationFlow
    -> arbiter-check proposed mutation
    -> apply mutation to topology registry
    -> return human-readable result + evidence
```

So the assistant becomes the outer `ILogicalOrchestrator`, while topology changes are handled by a logical flow, not by ad hoc methods.

**First Safe Implementation Phase**

Do not start with all mutations. Start with one:

`add_domain`

Phase shape:

1. Move logical contracts into `21.AgentInfrastructure/Logical`.
2. Add `ILogicalTopologyRegistry`.
3. Add in-memory registry with domains only.
4. Add `AddDomainLogicalUnit`.
5. Add `TopologyMutationFlow` supporting only `add_domain`.
6. Adapt `LogicalOrchestratorAssistant` to route `add domain ...` requests to that flow.
7. Prove full suite passes.

Then repeat for:

1. edit domain
2. add phase
3. edit phase
4. add sub-phase
5. edit sub-phase
6. add transition
7. edit transition

That gives you real adaptive orchestration without creating a giant unsafe rewrite.

> The analysis is correct and the recommended sequence is right. A few things are worth stating precisely before any implementation starts.
>
> **What the analysis gets exactly right.**
>
> The dependency direction problem is real and must be solved first. `35.ExperimentsV2` already references `21.AgentInfrastructure`. If `21` references `35` back, the build fails. Moving the contracts to `21.AgentInfrastructure/Logical` is the correct structural fix — it makes the contracts a runtime-layer artifact that everything can reference without creating a cycle. Project 35 becomes experiment proof against those contracts, not the owner of them. This is the same relationship that `OperationResult<T>` already has — it lives in `AgentInfrastructure.Core` and everything uses it.
>
> The identification of the proto-logical-units in projects 21-23 is accurate. `RouteClassifier`, `RoleBasedTaskDecomposer`, `KnnSkillFilter`, `InternalResultExaminer`, and `ExternalAiResultAdapter` are all unit-shaped already — they receive a defined input and produce a defined output. The gap is that they are not typed as `ILogicalUnit<TInput, TOutput>` and therefore cannot be registered, swapped, versioned, or evaluated against a conformance suite. Wrapping them as logical unit adapters before replacing their internals is the right approach — it is the same one-unit-presence-per-phase discipline that kept the E53 and T34 rounds clean.
>
> The `AgentStateMachine` observation is the most valuable one. It is already a flow runner — `AgentStateNode` is essentially an untyped logical unit, and the state machine traverses edges between nodes. The typed `AgentStateNode` → `ILogicalUnit` adapter and the `AgentStateMachine` → `ILogicalFlow` adapter are the path from the existing runtime behavior to the logical surface without rewriting anything.
>
> **What needs one more decision before the implementation starts.**
>
> The `TopologyMutationFlow` idea is structurally correct but the command shape needs tightening. The proposed `LogicalTopologyCommand` has an `Operation` string and a `TargetType` string. These will diverge as operations multiply. The safer shape is a discriminated union or a sealed hierarchy from the start:
>
> ```csharp
> public abstract record LogicalTopologyCommand(string Reason);
> public sealed record AddDomainCommand(LogicalDomain Domain, string Reason) : LogicalTopologyCommand(Reason);
> public sealed record EditPhaseCommand(string PhaseId, LogicalPhasePatch Patch, string Reason) : LogicalTopologyCommand(Reason);
> public sealed record AddTransitionCommand(LogicalTransition Transition, string Reason) : LogicalTopologyCommand(Reason);
> ```
>
> This matters because the `ILogicalFlow<LogicalTopologyCommand>` then knows at compile time which command it is handling rather than switching on strings at runtime. The units inside the topology mutation flow — `DomainMutationPlannerUnit`, `TransitionMutationPlannerUnit` — can be typed to specific command subtypes rather than handling a generic map.
>
> **The one concern about the proposed `LogicalOrchestratorAssistant` evolution.**
>
> The analysis proposes making `RunAsync` classify the request as either RunFlow or MutateTopology before routing. This is the right behavior but the classification itself is an `ILogicalUnit` — a `TopologyIntentClassifierUnit` with role `intent-classifier`. If the classification lives as a conditional inside `RunAsync`, it becomes a hardcoded routing rule that cannot be versioned, swapped, or retrained. The cleaner approach is that the orchestrator receives a request, routes it to the intent classifier unit, and the unit's output determines which flow runs next. This keeps the orchestrator as a selector, not a reasoner.
>
> **The recommended sequence as stated is correct with one reordering.**
>
> The analysis lists moving contracts first, then adding adapters, then adding the state machine flow, then topology mutation. That order is right. The one thing to add explicitly: the `ILogicalTopologyRegistry` must be implemented and tested before any mutation flow unit is written. Units that mutate topology cannot be written without knowing what mutation returns and what failure looks like. The registry is the contract the mutation units depend on, so it comes before any unit, not alongside it.
>
> Concretely: move contracts → implement `ILogicalTopologyRegistry` with add-domain only → write `AddDomainCommand` and the discriminated hierarchy → write the first topology mutation logical unit → wrap it in a one-step `TopologyMutationFlow` → adapt the assistant to route add-domain requests to that flow → full suite green. Then repeat per operation. That is the safe path.

Agreed. That refinement is the right locking point before code.

The corrected first implementation sequence should be:

1. Move logical contracts from `35.ExperimentsV2` into `21.AgentInfrastructure/Logical`.
2. Update `35.ExperimentsV2` and `15.OrchestratorModel` to use the runtime-owned contracts.
3. Add `ILogicalTopologyRegistry` in `21.AgentInfrastructure/Logical`.
4. Implement only add-domain support in an in-memory topology registry.
5. Add the discriminated command hierarchy, starting with:
   `LogicalTopologyCommand` and `AddDomainCommand`.
6. Add one logical unit:
   `AddDomainTopologyMutationUnit`.
7. Add one flow:
   `TopologyMutationFlow`, initially one-step and add-domain only.
8. Adapt `LogicalOrchestratorAssistant` so topology mutation goes through the logical flow, not through inline branching logic.
9. Add tests and run full suite after each phase.

And yes: the intent classifier must itself be a logical unit, not an `if` block inside `RunAsync`. The orchestrator should select and coordinate; it should not become the place where reasoning logic accumulates. That distinction matters if this is going to stay adaptive.

The first phase should be contract relocation only. No topology registry yet. That phase proves dependency direction is fixed without changing behavior. Then the topology registry comes next.

> The tool is a WPF application with three regions. > Why Helix Toolkit, not WPF native Viewport3D. The native Viewport3D requires you to write your own camera control, hit-testing, and mesh tessellation. Helix Toolkit wraps all three. The mesh builders (MeshBuilder.AddSphere, AddCylinder, AddBox) are the remaining primitives needed — every node type in the design is one of those three calls with different parameters. MIT license, clean NuGet install, no native DLL dependencies.
> The StationTrace record is the architectural centre. Everything the inspector needs — station name, kind, input property tree, output property tree, error code, timing, topology node id — is captured in one immutable record per station hop. The UI has no special knowledge of LogicalFlowResult or LogicalUnitResult; it only knows PropertyNode. The PropertyNodeSerialiser converts any object into that tree using reflection. Adding a new station type in the future requires no UI changes.
> The tracing decorators keep the real code untouched. TracingLogicalTopologyRegistry wraps InMemoryLogicalTopologyRegistry and emits traces on every call. TracingTopologyMutationFlow wraps TopologyMutationFlow and emits traces before and after delegating. The real assistant, real flow, and real registry run exactly as they do in tests. The inspector observes without interfering.
> The pulse animation is a sequential replay, not real-time. After all traces are collected synchronously, AnimatePulse iterates through them and sets ActiveNodeIds for 400 ms each. This is deliberate — real-time streaming through station transitions happens in microseconds, which would be invisible. The replay makes each hop legible.
> Twelve implementation phases, one panel at a time. The progression is: scaffold → data layer → tracing registry → full session wiring → scene builder → 3D viewport → scene update loop → signal trace panel → property tree control → pulse animation → hit-testing → command input bar. Each phase has a Gate B that is a specific build-and-run assertion.
