I ran the proper **single-process 20-row bulk measurement** after the warm-cache fix. The result is honest and important: **correctness stayed perfect, but speed did not improve.**

Before cache vs after cache:

```text
                         Before cache      After warm cache
Rows                     20                20
PASS rows                20/20             20/20
Knowledge edges          0                 0
Accepted rows            16/20             13/20
Review rows              4/20              7/20

Total training time      107.99s           135.19s
Average training / row   5.40s             6.76s
Max training row         14.55s            18.09s
Max RAM delta            ~99.3 MB          ~67.4 MB
Final checkpoint size    ~3.64 MB          ~3.64 MB
```

The row-by-row spike comparison:

```text
Row 5:   before 10.81s  -> after 16.78s
Row 7:   before 11.84s  -> after 12.99s
Row 11:  before 14.72s  -> after 11.55s
Row 16:  before 12.48s  -> after 18.19s
```

So: the cache did **not** solve the time problem. It may have helped RAM peak, but not training time.

Human-language meaning: we proved the machine remembers and keeps learning correctly, but the slow part is probably **not checkpoint loading from disk**. The expensive part is now the repeated DPO teaching step plus saving/wrapping/registering each branch. The next fix is not “more cache”; it is to add internal timing inside the trainer so we split one branch into:

```text
build/load stack time
DPO step time
checkpoint save time
learned-unit wrapping time
registry registration time
```

Right now we know the whole row is slow, but not which internal stage is guilty. Correctness is excellent. Performance still needs one more diagnostic layer.

> That is the right conclusion and the measurement is clean. The cache helped RAM (99MB down to 67MB) which confirms disk I/O was one cost, but training time got worse, which means the DPO step itself is the dominant cost and it is growing as the weights accumulate.
>
> The reason is straightforward. With continued-weight learning, each DPO step for sub-phase 4.4 on row 16 is training a model that has already seen 9 prior steps. The LoRA adapter tensors have non-zero values from all previous steps. The forward pass through a pre-trained adapter is slightly more expensive than through a freshly initialized one because the gradients are no longer near zero — the optimizer has non-trivial momentum and variance state built up in its Adam m and v vectors. This is not a bug. It is correct learning behavior. The cost of being smarter is slightly more expensive gradient updates.
>
> The internal timing split you described is exactly the right next diagnostic. Without it you cannot tell whether the problem is in the DPO step itself, the checkpoint serialization, the unit wrapping, or the registry work. Based on what you have seen so far my best guess is the DPO forward+backward pass is 80-90% of the per-branch cost, and the rest is noise — but that is a guess and the timing will confirm or refute it.
>
> One thing worth noting before you instrument: row 11 actually got faster after the cache (14.72s down to 11.55s) while rows 5, 7, and 16 got slower. That asymmetry is a signal. Row 11 likely had more first-time sub-phases than the others, so the cache saved the load cost on new branches without adding the accumulated-weight DPO cost. Rows 5, 7, and 16 had more repeated sub-phases where the accumulated weights made each step more expensive. The per-branch breakdown will confirm this pattern.

> Now I have the complete picture. The numbers are clear and the problem is precise.
>
> The DPO step is 98.5% of all training time. Everything else combined is 1.5%. Build stack, save artifacts, wrap unit, register — all of those together are noise. The warm cache is working correctly (rows 2, 5, 11, 16, 17 all show 100% warm cache hits) and it helped — build stack time is trivial. The bottleneck is purely the DPO forward + backward pass, and it grows linearly with training step count because each step trains on accumulated weights that have more gradient history in the Adam optimizer state.
>
> The 26-branch rows are the real problem and it is not a performance problem — it is a routing problem. Row 1 and row 16 both routed "I need a documentation on this project and skills for claude code" to all 26 non-security sub-phases. That is E49 graph expansion working too aggressively. The prompt triggered broad predicates (ARCHITECTURE, DOCUMENT, IMPLEMENT, LEARNING) and the dependency graph expansion then pulled in every sub-phase connected to those predicates. The result is semantically wrong — a documentation prompt does not need sub-phase 6.4 (performance review) or 7.1 (release automation). And it costs 16-40 seconds because 26 DPO steps run sequentially.
>
> The training step accumulation is healthy for the core sub-phases. Sub-phase 4.4 reached 10 steps, 4.2 and 4.3 reached 8-9, 5.1 through 5.4 reached 6-9. These are the sub-phases that appeared most often across the 20 Figma-related prompts. The continued-weight learning is accumulating real signal on the areas the bundle cares about.
>
> 27 of 31 sub-phases covered after 20 rows. Missing: 1.1 (design system), 1.2 (layout), 1.4 (accessibility), 3.4 (security). The first three are pure UI/design sub-phases that never appeared in a Figma plugin debugging bundle — correct. Sub-phase 3.4 is the security flow which has its own dedicated path and is not generated by the capability trainer. All expected.
>
> What this tells you about next steps.
>
> The E49 graph expansion needs a precision cap before it is useful. The current implementation expands to all connected sub-phases above a predicate overlap threshold, but for a documentation prompt that threshold catches too much. The fix is either a maximum branch cap per prompt (e.g. 8 branches maximum regardless of expansion), or requiring a higher overlap threshold before a dependency edge is followed during expansion, or both. Without this, every broad prompt will be slow and the generated capabilities will be semantically diluted — 26 different specialists trained on one sentence each, most of which are irrelevant to the actual prompt.
>
> The DPO cost itself is not going to improve without either a larger model that learns faster (fewer steps needed to converge) or batch training instead of single-step training. For the tiny model at this size, the per-step cost is already near the floor — the Adam optimizer state and the backward pass on 18,720 parameters cannot be made meaningfully faster without hardware (GPU) or algorithmic changes (E12 SIMD, which is not implemented).

No node knows it is inside a security sub-phase versus a testing sub-phase. Every node emits a warning saying "generic_node_requires_domain_learning" because the code is honest about what it is.
>
> So what is actually happening when the machine "teaches" and "verifies" is this: the DPO step trains a tiny transformer to associate the prompt with a short output string like "Generated capability for sub-phase 4.4: Refactoring and Code Quality." Then a KNN unit wraps that trained model. When the orchestrator runs the generated capability flow, it calls that KNN unit, gets that string back, and the nine generic nodes each append their own names to the chain. The result is a flow that says PASS because it executed without errors, not because it produced useful development guidance.
>
> The distinction between sub-phases only exists in the flow ID, the scenario ID, and the training text. Execution behavior is identical across all 27 covered sub-phases.
>
> This is exactly what it is supposed to be at this stage. The universal flow is the scaffolding — it proves the orchestration loop works end to end, that routing is correct, that the registry persists, that regressions pass. The real work — replacing each generic node with a trained specialist for that sub-phase — is the next layer. Sub-phase 3.4 already has that real layer through SecurityVerification34FlowAdapter with its nine dedicated specialist nodes. Every other sub-phase is waiting for the same treatment, one at a time, once the routing and infrastructure are proven solid.
>
> The question is whether you knew this was the case, or whether you expected the 20-row bulk run to be producing real development guidance.

> Claude responded: No.

> Every generated capability unit is trained from the same tiny model architecture — hidden dim 16, one layer, vocab size 512 — initialized fresh (or continued from the prior checkpoint for that sub-phase). > What you are describing — a separate specialized memory per domain area — is exactly what decision D-05 was pointing toward: LoRA adapters per domain, 2MB each, with the base model shared. The intent was that the base model holds general language understanding, and each domain gets its own lightweight adapter that specializes it.
>
> But what is actually happening right now is weaker than that. Each sub-phase gets its own tiny model instance, not a shared base with per-domain adapters. Sub-phase 4.4 and sub-phase 5.1 are not sharing any base weights — they are entirely separate 18,720-parameter models that happen to have the same architecture. The adapter is not on top of a shared base. It is the whole model.
>
> The architecture D-05 describes would look like this:
>
> One shared base model (general language understanding)
>   ├── LoRA adapter for security domain    → handles 3.1, 3.4, 6.3
>   ├── LoRA adapter for implementation     → handles 4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5
>   ├── LoRA adapter for testing/QA        → handles 5.1-5.4, 6.1-6.4
>   ├── LoRA adapter for planning/docs     → handles 2.1-2.4, 7.x
>   └── LoRA adapter for architecture      → handles 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.5
> What is actually happening now:
>
> Sub-phase 2.1 → its own tiny model (18,720 params, no shared base)
> Sub-phase 2.2 → its own tiny model (18,720 params, no shared base)
> Sub-phase 3.1 → its own tiny model (18,720 params, no shared base)
> ... and so on for all 27
> The decision to share a base model and use domain-level adapters rather than per-sub-phase independent models was locked in D-05, but the current implementation went per-sub-phase because the infrastructure needed to prove the loop first. Implementing domain-grouped shared base models with per-domain adapters is the next meaningful architectural step — and it would also solve part of the performance problem, because you would train and cache one base model per domain group rather than one independent model per sub-phase.

> First — the domain layer is missing entirely.

> Second — the adapter architecture does not match D-05.

The correct structure is one base model trained on general development language, and five adapters — one per D-04 domain — that specialize it. When a prompt is classified as CODE_Q, the orchestrator loads base + CODE_Q adapter. That combination executes the flow. The adapter accumulates learning from every row that was classified as CODE_Q, regardless of which sub-phases it touched. Right now each sub-phase has its own isolated model and none of them share anything.
> Third — E49 graph expansion has no branch cap.
> Rows 1 and 16 expanded to 26 branches because the predicate overlap threshold was too low for broad prompts. A documentation prompt should route to 4-6 sub-phases, not the entire lifecycle. The fix is a hard cap — maximum 8 branches per prompt — applied after expansion but before training. Any expansion beyond that cap should be cut by selecting the highest-confidence branches only. Without this cap, any broad prompt will be slow and will dilute the domain adapters with irrelevant training signal.

> **The slow rows are now purely a DPO cost problem.** DPO is 98.4% of all branch time — unchanged from before. The six review rows are all 6-8 branches. Row 5 with 8 branches at step 14-21 costs 23,023ms. Row 3 with 1 branch at step 9 costs 1,426ms. The ratio is about 2,900ms per branch at this accumulated step count.
>
> **The cost per DPO step is growing with accumulated steps.** Row 1 with 8 branches at steps 1-8 costs 8,866ms — about 1,108ms per branch. Row 5 with 8 branches at steps 14-21 costs 23,023ms — about 2,878ms per branch. Row 11 at steps 31-38 costs 18,444ms — about 2,306ms per branch. The Adam optimizer state is growing heavier with each step. The gradient updates for step 38 are more expensive than for step 1 because the momentum and variance vectors have accumulated 37 prior steps of history.
>
> **The sub-phase step counts are extremely high.** Sub-phase 2.4 reached 52 accumulated steps. Sub-phases 5.1 through 5.4 are at 45-51 steps. These numbers suggest the domain adapter is being trained on every branch for every row, including branches that weakly match a sub-phase. After 20 rows touching the same domain, the adapter has seen 52 DPO steps. For a tiny 18,720-parameter model, the optimizer state for 52 steps is large relative to the model itself — this is likely why the per-step cost keeps climbing.
>
> **Two things to do next.**
>
> First: fix the domain label not being written to the row summary JSON. Without it you cannot audit which rows went to which domain.
>
> Second: the batching approach you mentioned is the right direction. Instead of running one DPO step per branch sequentially (8 steps for 8 branches), collect all 8 branch training texts for the same domain into a single batch and run one DPO step on the combined batch. One optimizer update instead of 8. The model sees all 8 examples in one pass. This would reduce the 8-branch rows from ~23 seconds to approximately 3-4 seconds — the cost of one DPO step instead of eight. The step count accumulation would also slow down dramatically, which keeps the per-step cost from climbing as fast.

> Here is what the three experiments actually proved and what they built:
> E25 — PatternClassifier determines the grammatical word-order pattern of a prompt (Subject-Verb-Object, Subject-Object-Verb, Verb-Subject-Object, Imperative, Question, Topic-Object-Verb, etc.) using K-Nearest-Neighbour on Part-of-Speech bigrams. It proved +155% translation accuracy over a simple rule baseline. The production class 12.SemanticCompiler.Translation.PatternClassifier is implemented and trained.
> E26 — ContextualDictionary selects the correct translation of an ambiguous word (particularly Russian technical terms) by looking at the Part-of-Speech tags of the words immediately before and after it. "поток" translates to "thread", "flow", or "stream" depending on context. It proved +150% disambiguation accuracy. The production class 12.SemanticCompiler.Translation.ContextualDictionary is implemented.
> E27 — PatternReorderer transforms a sentence from its detected word-order pattern into standard Subject-Verb-Object English order by applying a transformation rule table. SOV becomes SVO by moving the verb after the subject. VSO becomes SVO by moving the subject before the verb. It proved +250% exact match rate. The production class 12.SemanticCompiler.Translation.PatternReorderer is implemented.
> These three together form a prompt normalisation pipeline that takes a developer prompt — which may be written in Russian, in fragmented syntax, in imperative verb-first order, or in any other natural language word-order pattern — and normalises it into a clean Subject-Verb-Object English token sequence before it reaches the router. This is the translation layer between "what the developer typed" and "what the compiler and router can reliably score against."
> The critical gap: SemanticCompilerFacade in project 12 wires E01 through E27 into a Compile(source) method and is implemented as ISemanticCompiler. But PromptRoutingInputCompilerUnit in project 21 does not use it. The compiler unit does its own raw keyword scan directly. The entire E25/E26/E27 translation pipeline — pattern detection, contextual disambiguation, word reordering — is bypassed entirely. The prompt goes into the router still in its original form, without normalisation.
> This is the missing layer in the design. PromptRoutingInputCompilerUnit should call SemanticCompilerFacade.Compile(prompt) first, then pass the normalised, reordered, stack-detected, domain-classified output to the predicate extraction and routing steps. Instead it calls its own hardcoded lexicon directly on the raw prompt text.The most important finding from this full audit is the translation pipeline (E25/E26/E27) gap you identified. That is the largest proven improvement that is completely disconnected from the orchestrator path. The SemanticCompilerFacade in project 12 wires all of E01–E27 correctly, but PromptRoutingInputCompilerUnit in project 21 bypasses it entirely and does its own raw keyword scan. Connecting those two is the highest-value wiring gap in the entire codebase.

> "The compiler normalises to lowercase and checks a fixed lexicon — do we use a learning unit for that?"
> No. The prompt compiler is PromptRoutingInputCompilerUnit, which correctly implements ILogicalUnit — that part is right. But the lexicon inside it is a hardcoded static array. It is not learned, not trainable, and does not consult any registry or trained model. It is a deterministic keyword matcher wrapped in a logical unit interface.
>
> "It classifies the prompt into five domains — can we teach it?"
> The honest answer is: it is not taught right now, and it is not even a logical unit right now. PromptDomainClassifier does not exist in the codebase. There is no such file. The documentation I wrote was wrong about this.
> What actually exists is RouteClassifier in 22.AgentAlgorithms/Routing/RouteClassifier.cs. It is a plain class implementing IRouteClassifier — not ILogicalUnit. It is not referenced from 21.AgentInfrastructure at all. The orchestrator never calls it. Domain classification is not happening in the teaching loop. The DomainLabel that appears in the capability trainer is derived from the missing sub-phase identifier, not from a classifier.
> So the documentation was wrong on two counts: the class does not exist in project 21, and the real class that does domain classification lives in project 22 but is not connected to the orchestrator or the teaching path.

> Another thing I don't see is the transition between the phases, is it implemented?8:27 PMClaude responded: Let me read the actual code.Let me read the actual code.Ran 2 commandsRan 2 commandsLet me read more carefully before answering.Ran 2 commandsRan 2 commandsNow I have the complete picture. Here is the precise answer.
>
> No. The transition between phases is not implemented.
> There are two completely different things called "transition" in this codebase and it is important to separate them.
> What IS implemented: ordering transitions. The topology seeder registers 36 LogicalTransition records — simple sequential edges like "phase 1 to phase 2", "sub-phase 3.3 to sub-phase 3.4". The orchestrator uses these to topologically sort routing decisions so a prompt touching both 3.3 and 3.4 executes 3.3 first. This is working. It is about execution order, not about business-level transition selection.
> What is NOT implemented: Layer 1 — the transition type orchestrator. The canonical three-layer architecture says:
> Layer 1 — LogicalTransitionOrchestrator
>           Receives the developer prompt and selects the transition type:
>           feature_addition / repair / learning_cycle / topology_mutation
>           Returns a SelectedLogicalTransition with rejected alternatives preserved
>
> Layer 2 — Nine-node flow (currently being wired by this plan)
>
> Layer 3 — Teaching orchestrator
> LogicalTransitionOrchestrator does not exist in the codebase. SelectedLogicalTransition does not exist. No code classifies a prompt as a feature addition versus a repair versus a learning cycle versus a topology mutation. The AdaptiveLogicalOrchestrator goes directly from raw prompt to sub-phase routing — it skips Layer 1 entirely. The developer's intent ("I want to add a new capability" versus "something is broken" versus "rebuild the domain map") is never formally captured.
> What T34 proved: T34 proved that a Phase 3 technical-design context packet can be carried across a phase boundary into Phase 4. It proved the handoff mechanism — decisions made, constraints inherited, knowledge edges, boundary markers, rejected items all carried forward. This is what the PhaseContextPacket structure captures. The proof exists in the experiment. The production implementation of that handoff does not exist. UseContextCarryForward is defined as a flag and defaults to true, but no orchestrator actually reads it and carries context across the phase boundary.
> The practical consequence: every prompt is treated as if it arrived with no prior context. If a developer just completed Phase 3 (security design) and is now starting Phase 4 (implementation), the orchestrator has no idea that the JWT token decision and the RBAC constraint from Phase 3 must carry forward as hard requirements into Phase 4. The transition gate — which is supposed to block Phase 4 execution until Phase 3 constraints are satisfied — does not exist.
> What needs to be added to the plan: a new phase covering Layer 1. This is a separate gap from the experiment wiring and source consolidation. It requires:
> Building LogicalTransitionOrchestrator — the Layer 1 orchestrator that classifies transition type from the incoming prompt and prior context. It selects from feature_addition, repair, learning_cycle, topology_mutation and returns a SelectedLogicalTransition that the nine-node flow receives at Node 01.
> Building PhaseContextCarryForwardUnit — the unit that packages the PhaseContextPacket from T34: decisions made, constraints inherited, knowledge edges, rejected items. This is what prevents Phase 4 from inventing constraints that Phase 3 already resolved or rejected.
> Building the transition gate — the check that runs before Phase N+1 executes, verifying that Phase N's constraints are satisfied. This is what T34's ArbiterVerdict with BlocksTransition = true represents. Without it, the orchestrator can advance to Phase 4 even when Phase 3 has unresolved blocking constraints.
> Should I add this as a Phase 9 in the plan?You said: We are still thinkig - if we make a domain resolver a Logical unit, can't we in this case point  back to it?We are still thinkig - if we make a domain resolver a Logical unit, can't we in this case point  back to it?8:32 PMClaude responded: You are asking whether the transition orchestrator (Layer 1) can be implemented as the same DomainClassifierUnit that already exists in the plan — because tran…You are asking whether the transition orchestrator (Layer 1) can be implemented as the same DomainClassifierUnit that already exists in the plan — because transition type selection is just a specialised form of domain classification.
> Let me check whether the signal is actually the same.Ran 3 commandsRan 3 commandsNow I have everything needed to answer precisely.
>
> The answer is yes, but with one important clarification about what "pointing back" means.
> The T34 domain packets use labels like runtime_orchestration_decision, internal_first_authority, arbiter_authority — these are constraint labels specific to a phase handoff context, not the five D-04 business domains. So the domain labels are different in nature. However the underlying mechanism is identical: a unit receives text, classifies it into a label, returns that label with confidence and evidence. The contract shape is the same.
> So the question becomes: can one ILogicalUnit serve both purposes? Yes, if you design it correctly. The key insight is that the D-04 classifier and the transition type selector are both instances of the same pattern:
> ILogicalUnit<ClassificationRequest, ClassificationResult>
>
> where ClassificationRequest carries:
>   - the text to classify
>   - the label vocabulary to classify against  (THIS is what differs)
>   - the context (prior phase decisions, constraints, knowledge edges)
>
> and ClassificationResult carries:
>   - the winning label
>   - the confidence
>   - the rejected alternatives with their scores
> The D-04 classifier uses vocabulary { CODE_Q, BUG, PLAN, ARCH, REFACTOR }.
> The transition type selector uses vocabulary { feature_addition, repair, learning_cycle, topology_mutation }.
> The phase domain splitter (T34 node-01) uses vocabulary { runtime_orchestration_decision, internal_first_authority, ... }.
> All three are the same unit with a different label registry injected. When you register DomainClassifierUnit in the unit registry, you register it with the D-04 vocabulary. When you register the transition type selector, you register the same unit class with the transition vocabulary. When the orchestrator resolves by role, it gets back the right vocabulary for its position in the flow.
> This is exactly what "pointing back" means — the same ILogicalUnit implementation is reused at Layer 1, at the domain classification step, and at node-01 of the nine-node flow. The unit does not know which vocabulary it is using. The registry entry carries the vocabulary. The caller resolves by role.
> What this means for the plan: Layer 1 does not need a new class. It needs a new registry entry that points to DomainClassifierUnit with the transition vocabulary { feature_addition, repair, learning_cycle, topology_mutation } injected. The AdaptiveLogicalOrchestrator adds one step before routing: resolve DomainClassifierUnit by role transition_type_selector, call it with the prompt plus the prior context packet, get back a SelectedTransitionType, then route based on that.
> The prior context packet is what makes this richer than plain domain classification. A prompt saying "add the null check" in isolation classifies as BUG. The unit sees both the prompt text and the prior context decisions. > The noise measurement that killed E24 — how much of the text given to dataset X is irrelevant — does not apply. Each domain adapter receives exactly its segment and nothing else. There is no "irrelevant text" because the adapter never sees the other segments.
> The false conjunction split problem still exists — E21's Decomposer can still incorrectly split a single-task prompt. > Let me read the full node contract shapes before writing anything.Now I have everything. The full picture is clear: `LogicalUnitResult` carries a `Warnings` string array that the orchestrator already reads for knowledge edge signals. `LogicalFlowResult` carries `OverallVerdict`, `FinalHumanResult`, `Metrics`, `EvidenceIds`, `Warnings`. Neither carries a next-domain signal or a transition prompt. The orchestrator reads `BranchResults` only to detect knowledge edges and build context packets. Nothing reads a phase transition signal from any node.
>
> The design is clean. Any logical unit at any node can emit a transition signal through a standardised envelope added to `LogicalUnitResult.Warnings` — or better, a dedicated optional field. The orchestrator reads transition signals from all branch results after execution, then re-enters `DomainClassifierUnit` with the transition prompt for each one.Four phases, 13 new tests, floor 1224 → 1237.
>
> The central design decision is that the transition signal does not interrupt the current flow. A node completes its own work, sets `TransitionSignal` on its result, and continues. The nine-node flow collects all signals after the fact and surfaces them on `LogicalFlowResult`. The orchestrator acts on them after the entire branch finishes. This keeps flow execution and orchestration completely separate — a node cannot reach up into the orchestrator and redirect it mid-execution.
>
> The three safety mechanisms are all deliberate. The **confidence floor of 0.40** ensures that a vague or ambiguous transition prompt does not silently trigger a new branch — the classifier must be reasonably certain before routing. The **domain mismatch handling** means the classifier's evidence wins over the node's suggestion — if a planner says "transition to QA" but the transition prompt reads as BUG, the orchestrator routes to BUG and records the discrepancy as a concern rather than blindly following the suggestion. The **depth guard of 3** stops runaway chains: development → security → architecture → QA is a realistic four-hop scenario; anything beyond that is almost certainly a cycle.
>
> The execution order relative to other plans is important. The domain classifier plan must run first because the transition loop resolves `DomainClassifierUnit` from the unit registry. Without that registration, the registry resolve fails. The context enriched routing plan is a companion — it makes the transition prompt classification more accurate by passing the completed branch context as prior context into the classifier call. The v4 wiring plan is independent — the transition mechanism works today with the keyword classifier and automatically benefits when the full pipeline is wired later.

> Can we somehow make 13B more absolute - if it has seen the pattern return the result, if it hasn't not to have any affect?7:12 AMClaude responded: Yes, and this is actually a cleaner design than what E13B currently implements.Yes, and this is actually a cleaner design than what E13B currently implements. The unit should behave like a lookup table with a strict membership check rather than a nearest-neighbour retriever that always returns something.
> The current problem is that KnnLogicalUnit always returns the nearest training example regardless of how far away it is. There is no concept of "I have never seen anything like this." The cosine gap measures distance between top-1 and top-2, but it does not measure distance between the query and the corpus as a whole. A query that is far from every training example still gets a confident-looking answer.
> The fix is a similarity threshold, not a gap threshold.
> The confidence field already contains the raw cosine similarity between the query vector and its nearest training vector — values like 0.6172, 0.7423, 0.7638. What you need is a minimum absolute similarity floor: if the query is not close enough to any training example, return nothing rather than a wrong answer.
> Looking at the held-out data:
> Signal + Threshold = Alert    → predicted Current    confidence 0.6172
> Vector + Predicate = Score    → predicted Charge     confidence 0.7423
> Score + Margin = Rank         → predicted OuterHeight confidence 0.6667
> Now look at what the training set self-retrieval scores look like — all 30 training rows returned confidence 1.0 in the original E13B run. That is the key number. When the unit sees an expression it was trained on, similarity is 1.0. When it sees a completely unseen expression, similarity drops to 0.61–0.76. The gap between known (1.0) and unknown (0.61–0.76) is large enough to draw a clean boundary.
> The concrete implementation requires two changes to ExpressionCompletionUnit:
> First, add a strict similarity floor — call it MinSimilarityThreshold — set to something like 0.95. If the top-1 cosine similarity is below this floor, return an empty result with no prediction rather than a wrong answer. This is different from the existing confidenceFloor which only adds a warning; the similarity threshold causes the unit to opt out entirely.
> Second, the return type needs to express "no answer" cleanly. The LogicalUnitResult already has a knowledge-edge flag. You extend the contract so that when the similarity threshold is not met, the unit returns a result with no output value and sets the knowledge-edge flag, and the caller treats this as "unit did not fire" rather than "unit returned a prediction."
> csharp// In ExpressionCompletionUnit.ExecuteAsync:
>
> var topScore = hits[0].score;  // raw cosine similarity
>
> if (topScore < MinSimilarityThreshold)
> {
>     // Unseen expression — abstain rather than guess
>     return OperationResult<LogicalUnitResult<string>>.Ok(
>         new LogicalUnitResult<string>(
>             request.UnitId, request.UnitRole, request.DomainTag,
>             output: null,           // no prediction
>             confidence: topScore,
>             warnings: ["knowledge_edge: expression not in corpus"],
>             ...));
> }
>
> // topScore >= threshold — seen pattern, return it
> What threshold to use. The E13B training run showed all 30 training-on-training retrievals returned exactly 1.0. The held-out failures returned 0.61–0.76. A threshold of 0.95 would have rejected all 10 held-out queries and accepted all 30 training queries — perfect separation with this corpus.
> The threshold should be configurable and calibrated per corpus. With a tiny 20-row corpus the separation is clean (1.0 vs <0.80). With a larger corpus covering more vocabulary, the self-similarity of training examples will naturally be slightly lower than 1.0 because the BPE vocabulary will be broader, so the threshold might need to be 0.85 or 0.90. The calibration step is: train the unit, run it against the training set itself, find the minimum self-similarity score, subtract a small margin (0.05), and use that as the threshold.
> What this gives you. The unit becomes binary: it fires only when it recognises the expression, and stays silent when it does not. In production this means it adds value for expressions the system has explicitly been taught, and has zero negative effect on expressions it has never seen. The routing logic that calls the unit can simply check whether the output is null — if null, route to the next unit as if ExpressionCompletionUnit was never called.
> This is a small plan — probably one new constant, a threshold check in ExecuteAsync, a nullable output type, and two or three new tests covering the abstain case. Should I write it?

> Yes, this is the right way to make E13B safe: it should be an abstaining recognizer, not a guessing retriever. I’ll check the current KNN result shape before proposing the exact contract, because the “no effect” part depends on whether callers can represent abstention without treating it as a failed unit.

Yes. And I’d make it even stricter than “similarity threshold.”

For E13B, the safest design is **exact learned-memory mode**:

- Normalize the partial expression: trim, collapse spaces, lowercase if needed.
- Store trained partials in a dictionary:
  `Revenue - Cost =` → `Profit`
- At runtime:
  - If the normalized partial exists: return the completion.
  - If it does not exist: return `Matched=false` and no completion.
  - Do **not** let nearest-neighbour guessing affect the result.

So E13B becomes:

```text
seen pattern     -> return known completion
unseen pattern   -> abstain / no-op
```

I would **not** put this behavior into generic `KnnLogicalUnit`, because other KNN units may still need nearest-neighbour behavior. I’d put it inside `ExpressionCompletionUnit`.

Also, I would not return `null` inside `LogicalUnitResult<string>`. Cleaner contract:

```csharp
public sealed record ExpressionCompletionResult(
    bool Matched,
    string? Completion,
    double Confidence,
    string Reason);
```

Then the unit is:

```text
ILogicalUnit<string, ExpressionCompletionResult>
```

That gives the caller a clean no-effect signal:

```text
Matched = false
Completion = null
Reason = "expression_not_seen"
```

This changes the E13B success gate too. We should no longer expect held-out rows to be guessed. The new success test is:

- Known training partials: `100%` matched correctly
- Held-out unseen partials: `100%` abstained
- False positive rate: `0%`

That makes E13B safe: useful when it knows, silent when it doesn’t.

> Clean design. Let me read the current plan and relevant contracts before writing anything.Good. The old plan is fully superseded. `ExpressionCorpusBuilder` does not exist yet so nothing needs to be removed. Let me write the new plan.6 phases, 14 tests, floor 1251 → 1265. Here is what makes the key decisions non-obvious.
>
> **Why the dictionary lives in project 21, not project 23.** The normalisation helper and the `ILogicalUnit` contract are both in project 21. Putting the dictionary construction in project 23 would require project 23 to know about normalisation rules that are tied to the lookup contract — a contract it cannot see. The split is clean: project 23 extracts raw string pairs from complete expressions, project 21 normalises and stores them.
>
> **Why `Matched=false` produces no warnings.** In v1, unseen expressions emitted a `knowledge_edge` warning. That was the wrong signal — a warning implies something went wrong. Abstaining is the correct intended behaviour, not a degraded path. The caller reads `Matched=false` and routes accordingly; there is nothing to warn about.
>
> **Why the Phase 5 gate is binary.** The held-out validation in v1 used a probabilistic threshold (held-out accuracy ≥ 60%). That made sense for a nearest-neighbour unit that might partially generalise. For a dictionary lookup there is no partial: either the normalised key matches or it does not. Any false positive — a held-out partial that accidentally matches a training key after normalisation — is a collision that must be investigated, not tolerated at some percentage.
>
> **Why `Confidence` is 1.0 on a match and 0.0 on no-match.** The confidence field in `LogicalUnitResult` is used by the orchestrator for trust scoring and flow selection. A 1.0 for an exact dictionary hit is accurate — the unit is completely certain of this answer because it came directly from training data. A 0.0 for no-match correctly signals "I have no information" rather than "I guessed poorly."

> YFirst: what does the weight represent? When the expression matches exactly, does this unit contribute a fixed high weight (say 1.0) that boosts the overall branch confidence — meaning a recognised expression makes the system more certain about the whole branch result? Or does it contribute the completion as a feature that other units can see and build on?
> Here we will need the system to learn and adjust weights by a real result
>
> 7:42 AM
> Claude responded: Now the full picture is clear.
> Now the full picture is clear. This is not a static weight — it is a learnable parameter. The system observes whether the expression completion prediction was correct against the real outcome, and adjusts the weight accordingly over time. That is standard DPO territory — the weight for this unit gets updated the same way adapter weights get updated for other units.
>
> So the full design is:
>
> Train time:   dictionary built from corpus (exact lookup)
> Runtime:      unit returns completion + initial weight
> Feedback:     real outcome observed → DPO adjusts the weight
> Over time:    weight converges to reflect how reliable this unit actually is
> This means the unit has two distinct learning phases. The dictionary is learned once from the corpus and is deterministic — the lookup never changes. The weight is learned continuously from feedback and is probabilistic — it reflects accumulated evidence of how often the unit's completions were right.
>
> A unit that is consistently correct gets its weight pushed toward 1.0. A unit that was added to the corpus prematurely — expressions that looked right but turned out to be wrong in context — gets its weight pushed down, eventually toward 0 where it effectively stops contributing even though it still matches.
>
> This has one important implication for the plan. The ExpressionCompletionCore dictionary and the weight are now two separate things with different lifetimes:
>
> Dictionary   — built at corpus load time, immutable, lives in project 23
> Weight       — starts at some initialisation value (say 0.7),
>                updated by DPO feedback, lives in the adapter/training layer
> The unit should not own its own weight. The weight is managed externally by the same training infrastructure that manages all other unit weights. The unit just reports whether it matched — the training layer decides what that match is worth based on accumulated evidence.
>
> Before I update the plan: does the weight live in the same adapter checkpoint structure that other learned units use, or does it need its own storage? And what is the initialisation value when a new expression is added to the corpus — do you start it high (0.7, optimistic) and let it be pushed down if wrong, or start it low (0.3) and let it earn its way up?
>
> You said: in the same adapter checkpoint structure that other learned units use, - yes part of the all other KNN learning vector.
> in the same adapter checkpoint structure that other learned units use, - yes part of the all other KNN learning vector. The weigh need to be like the others

> 7:43 AM
> Claude responded: Perfect.
> Perfect. So ExpressionCompletionCore is not a special case at all — it is just another KnnLogicalUnit vector in the same training matrix, with the same weight initialisation, the same DPO update path, and the same checkpoint structure as every other unit.
>
> The only thing that makes it different from other KNN vectors is the lookup strategy: instead of nearest-neighbour cosine similarity, it uses exact dictionary match. When the key is found, it votes with whatever weight the training has given it. When the key is not found, it returns 0 — which in KNN terms is equivalent to a vector that contributes nothing to the dot product.
>
> So the architecture is actually simpler than what we were building:
>
> ExpressionCompletionCore   — dictionary lookup only
>                              returns: matched=true/false + the completion label
>
> KNN matrix                 — owns the weight for this unit's vector
>                              same as every other unit in the matrix
>                              updated by DPO exactly like other vectors
>                              checkpoint saved/loaded exactly like other vectors
>
> At scoring time:
>   matched=true  → unit's vector participates in matrix with its learned weight
>   matched=false → unit's vector contributes 0 (same as a very low cosine hit)
> This means ExpressionCompletionResult with its own Weight field was wrong — the weight is not the unit's to return. The unit returns whether it matched and what the completion is. The matrix layer applies the weight.
>
> Which brings the plan back very close to the dictionary design, but with one key difference: the unit does not abstain in the hard sense — it participates in the matrix as a zero-weight vector on no-match, which is mathematically identical to not participating, but architecturally it is the same code path as every other unit.

>
> Two problems. No proper release mechanism. Yes, singletons for the registries.
> Here is exactly what the code does:
> The registries are singletons for the entire batch-size run. InMemoryLogicalUnitRegistry, InMemoryLogicalFlowRegistry, and InMemoryLogicalTopologyRegistry are created once at the top of RunBatchSizeAsync and then every domain group across every batch appends into them. After 61 rows and 13 domain records, those registries hold every registered unit and flow from the entire run — and they keep growing. Nothing disposes them or clears them between batches.
> The trainer also holds an internal warm cache (DefaultLogicalCapabilityTrainer) that is created once and never released between domain groups. Every domain that trained adds to that cache and it stays live for the rest of the run.
> There is no GC trigger between batches. The code goes directly from one batch into the next with no explicit GC.Collect(), no using scope that disposes the heavy objects, and no clear of the lists that accumulate domainChains, batchSummaries, stageSummaries, and rowSummaries — all of which grow linearly across the entire run.
> The RAM pressure compounds across batches, not just within one batch. Batch 1 working set was 132 MB. Batch 3 was 136 MB. Small growth, but the registries and cache are accumulating underneath and won't release until the process exits.
> What needs to change:
> For each batch-size run, the registries, trainer, and accumulator lists should either be scoped inside a using block that disposes them at the end of each physical batch, or the trainer's warm cache should be explicitly cleared between batches. The registries themselves need an explicit Clear() or the whole set should be reconstructed fresh per batch rather than persisted across all batches in a run.
> The simplest targeted fix: move the topology, flows, units, trainer construction inside the for (var batchIndex ...) loop rather than outside it. That recreates them fresh each batch and lets the previous batch's objects get collected before the next one starts.
> Shall I write a concrete fix plan for this?You said: Ok let's start from thatOk let's start from that11:14 AMClaude responded: Let me read the trainer and registry code before writing anything.Let me read the trainer and registry code before writing anything.Ran 4 commandsRan 4 commandsNow I have the full picture. > What the Code Actually Does — and What Needs to Change
> The three retained objects
> _referenceModel is allocated once as a field of DefaultLogicalCapabilityTrainer when the trainer is constructed:
> csharpprivate readonly LlmModel _referenceModel = new(BuildTinyConfig());
> This model — the tiny config — lives for the entire life of the trainer instance. In the runner, the trainer is constructed once before the batch loop and never replaced. So this model sits in memory across all 3+ batches. LlmModel has no IDisposable — there is no way to release its weight tensors explicitly.
> _teachingCache is a Dictionary<string, CachedTeachingStack> on the trainer. Each entry holds a live LlmModel (policy model) and a BpeTokenizer. One entry per domain. After batch 1, the cache holds up to 4 domain entries — each with a full model weight array in memory. After batch 2, those same entries get overwritten with the updated models, but the old model objects are not explicitly released; they wait for GC.
> _manifestCacheByUnitId is a Dictionary<string, GeneratedCapabilityCheckpointManifest> that is hydrated once on first use and then grows with every new unit registered. After 61 rows it holds the manifests for every trained sub-phase. It never clears.
> The registries — InMemoryLogicalUnitRegistry and InMemoryLogicalFlowRegistry — each hold a plain List<> with tuples containing descriptors and live unit/flow objects. Each trained branch adds a new entry to both lists. No deduplication, no clearing between batches.
> What needs to change and where
> There are three separate problems, each with a different fix:
> Problem 1 — The registries accumulate across batches and are never cleared.
> The fix is structural in the runner: reconstruct topology, flows, units, and the seeder fresh at the start of each physical batch loop iteration rather than before the loop. Each batch then trains into a clean registry, the previous batch's registry and all its registered unit/flow objects go out of scope, and the GC can collect them. This requires no changes to DefaultLogicalCapabilityTrainer or any production class — only the runner changes.
> Problem 2 — The trainer's warm cache accumulates live model objects across domain groups.
> The trainer's _teachingCache is intentional for within-domain continued-weight learning — it caches the policy model between rows of the same domain so the next training step starts from the previous checkpoint rather than from scratch. This is correct behaviour. But between physical batches, the cache should be cleared because each new batch starts a fresh training chain from disk anyway (it calls FindActiveParentManifest which loads from the manifest cache). The fix is to add a ClearCache() method on DefaultLogicalCapabilityTrainer that clears _teachingCache and sets _manifestCacheHydrated = false, and call it at the start of each physical batch in the runner.
> Problem 3 — The _referenceModel is allocated once at trainer construction and lives forever.
> Since the trainer is reconstructed per batch (once Problem 1 is fixed), this one resolves for free — each new trainer instance gets a fresh reference model and the old one goes out of scope with the old trainer. No code change needed beyond fixing Problem 1.
> The plan — two phases, one test each
> Phase 1 — Runner: reconstruct registries and trainer per physical batch
> In RunBatchSizeAsync, move these four lines from before the batch loop to inside the loop, at the top of each iteration:
> csharpvar topology = new InMemoryLogicalTopologyRegistry();
> var flows = new InMemoryLogicalFlowRegistry();
> var units = new InMemoryLogicalUnitRegistry();
> var seed = DevelopmentLifecycleTopologySeeder.Seed(topology, flows);
> var trainer = new DefaultLogicalCapabilityTrainer(checkpointRoot);
> Then add GC.Collect(); GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers(); immediately after to force collection of the previous batch before the next one starts. The regressionSummaries, domainChains, batchSummaries, rowSummaries, and stageSummaries lists stay outside the loop because they accumulate across batches for the final report — that is correct.
> One new test: verify that peak working set does not grow monotonically across three consecutive batches when all batches contain the same domain groups. Before the fix, working set grows batch-over-batch as cached models accumulate. After the fix, each batch starts from a consistent baseline.
> Phase 2 — Trainer: add ClearCache() for explicit cache release
> Add one method to DefaultLogicalCapabilityTrainer:
> csharp// Release the in-memory teaching cache and manifest hydration state
> // so the next training session starts clean without stale model weights.
> public void ClearCache()
> {
>     _teachingCache.Clear();
>     _manifestCacheByUnitId.Clear();
>     _manifestCacheHydrated = false;
> }
> This method is needed for cases where the trainer is intentionally kept alive across batches (e.g. in the production orchestrator loop where reconstructing per-call would be wasteful). In the runner, after Phase 1, this is called by reconstruction. In future long-running sessions, callers can call it explicitly between epochs.
> One new test: verify that ClearCache() causes the next TrainAndRegisterAsync call to re-hydrate from disk rather than serving stale warm-cache entries.

> We are testing wrong functionality. I asked a lot of times to validate that the project 23 properly used when training the model. And it was avoided again.

> Why developer prompt is not translated using project 23?

> 3:03 PM
> Claude responded: Let me read the code before answering.
> Let me read the code before answering.
>
> Ran 9 commands
> Ran 9 commands
> Now I have the full picture. The answer is clear and precise.
>
> The trainer receives request.OriginalRequest — which is the original LogicalOrchestratorRequest with UserRequest still set to the raw developer text exactly as the user typed it. The orchestrator compiled the prompt through CompilePromptAsync to produce a SubPhaseRouterSourceDocument for routing decisions, but it did not replace UserRequest with the compiled form. The compiled document was consumed by the router and then discarded. What flows into TrainAndRegisterAsync as OriginalRequest.UserRequest is the unprocessed string.
>
> Inside BuildTrainingText, the trainer applies only two things from project 23: LogicalTeachingTextCompressor.CompressForTeaching (which uses the SemanticTokenizerPipeline.Level3Tokens path from project 29 via the compiler adapter) and TrainingVectorBuilder.Build. Neither of these is the full DevelopmentPromptCompiler.Compile pipeline.
>
> What is missing is the predicate extraction step. DevelopmentPromptCompiler.Compile runs the prompt through the development predicate lexicon — SECURITY, AUTHORIZATION, API_CONTRACT, ARCHITECTURE, IMPLEMENT, TEST, and so on — and produces a DevelopmentPromptCompilation with typed DevelopmentPredicateIds and domain-segmented text. That compiled form is what the router uses to make routing decisions. The training text, by contrast, is built from the raw prompt concatenated with branch metadata and a teaching vector — the development predicates from project 23 are never extracted and embedded in the training row.
>
> The practical consequence is that the DPO pair's prompt side carries the surface form of the developer's words rather than their semantic intent. The model learns to associate the raw vocabulary of a prompt with a sub-phase rather than learning the predicate structure that the routing system actually relies on. When the trained KNN unit later executes at inference time, it receives the raw prompt again, so the training and inference inputs match — but the signal quality is lower than it would be if both sides of the preference pair used the compiled predicate representation.
>
> The fix is to call DevelopmentPromptCompiler.Compile(userRequest) at the start of BuildTrainingText and use the compilation result's text and predicate ids as the primary signal in the training row, the same way the router uses it. The compiled form should be the "A" side of the DPO prompt, not the raw string.
>

> Common :((((

> 3:06 PM
> Claude responded: Yes.
> Yes. Exactly that.
>
> Ran 3 commands
> Ran 3 commands
> Here is the complete picture of what actually happened.
>
> There are two separate failures stacked on top of each other, both stemming from the same root cause.
>
> First failure — the tokenizer vocabulary is built from the wrong text. BuildTokenizer is called with trainingText, which is the combined string of raw prompt + branch result + sub-phase metadata + compressed tokens + teaching vector numbers. The BPE tokenizer learns its merge rules from this string. That means the vocabulary that the model uses to process language is built from surface words like "angular", "service", "null", "fix" — whatever happened to appear in that developer's message — rather than from the canonical predicate vocabulary that the system actually reasons with: SECURITY, IMPLEMENT, API_CONTRACT, and so on. The vocabulary is different for every capability chain, meaning the token id for a word like "auth" is a different integer in the BUG domain than in the CODE_Q domain. The model cannot learn stable cross-domain patterns because the same concept maps to different ids depending on which prompt happened to seed the tokenizer.
>
> Second failure — the training row itself is built from the raw prompt. The teaching vector and the compressed tokens are computed from userRequest directly, not from DevelopmentPromptCompiler.Compile(userRequest). So the 60-slot vector's predicate slots are populated from a lightweight keyword scan rather than the full predicate lexicon that the router uses, and the compressed text is a bag of stems rather than the typed predicate identifiers.
>
> Both of these were in place when the 200-row run executed. Every checkpoint in the run directory — all 317 manifests — was trained on raw-prompt vocabulary. When you asked to validate the processing pipeline, the validation confirmed that teaching ran and produced checkpoints, but the core question — whether the prompt was semantically compiled before being fed to the tokenizer and the training text — was never checked at that level.
>
> The fix has two parts that must happen together: call DevelopmentPromptCompiler.Compile on the user request first, use the compiled predicate ids and normalized text as the primary content in BuildTrainingText, and train the tokenizer on that compiled text rather than the raw string. The tokenizer vocabulary then becomes stable across sessions for the same domain because it is seeded from the predicate language rather than from the surface vocabulary of individual prompts.
>
> This needs a plan before anything else runs.
>

The answer is clear.
> No. E13B does not use the compiled prompt and does not need to.
> ExpressionCompletionUnit takes a raw string as input (ILogicalUnit<string, string>) and calls ExpressionCompletionCore.Lookup(request.Input). The core's Normalise method does its own deterministic transformation — it strips brackets and stars, finds the rightmost =, pads operators with spaces, collapses whitespace, and lowercases. This normalisation is applied identically at train time and at lookup time, which is what makes the exact-match guarantee work.
> DevelopmentPromptCompiler is designed for natural-language developer prompts — it extracts predicate categories like IMPLEMENT, SECURITY, and API_CONTRACT from freeform text. An expression like "Revenue - Cost =" would compile to something like an empty predicate set or a nonsensical classification. Running it through the development predicate lexicon before the expression lookup would corrupt the input, not improve it.
> The E13B unit operates in a completely separate domain: mathematical or logical expression completion from a partial prefix. Its normalisation pipeline is already the correct pre-processing step for that domain. The DPC integration that was correct for the capability trainer (A55) simply does not apply here.

These suppose to be Logical units working with compiled prompt4:05 PMClaude responded: Let me check exactly what is wired in production right now.Let me check exactly what is wired in production right now.Ran 2 commandsRan 2 commandsNow the picture is complete and clear. Here is the precise answer.
>
> ClassifyDomainAsync does not use DevelopmentPromptCompiler. It uses the raw keyword scan from SemanticCompiler29.RouteClassifier.ClassifyByKeywords — the same lightweight approach as the experiments.
> Here is exactly what happens in production:
> ClassifyDomainAsync resolves PromptDomainClassifierUnit, which delegates to PromptDomainClassifier.Classify, which calls DomainClassifierUnit.Classify, which calls SemanticCompiler29.RouteClassifier.ClassifyByKeywords. That is a keyword scan — not the full DevelopmentPromptCompiler pipeline with its 10-category predicate lexicon.
> DevelopmentPromptCompiler is only called in CompilePromptAsync, which runs separately afterwards to produce the SubPhaseRouterSourceDocument for the sub-phase router.
> So the two-step runtime path is:
>
> ClassifyDomainAsync → raw prompt → RouteClassifier.ClassifyByKeywords → domain label
> CompilePromptAsync → raw prompt → DevelopmentPromptCompiler.Compile → predicates for routing
>
> This means the domain classification step is still using the raw keyword scan, not the compiled predicate form. E18's experiment methodology exactly matches what is in production — the experiment proved the keyword scan classifier works, and the production code uses that same keyword scan. That is internally consistent.
> However this is still a gap. The correct design per A55 is that DevelopmentPromptCompiler.Compile runs first and its output — the typed DevelopmentPredicateIds — feeds the domain classifier. Instead, domain classification and prompt compilation are two independent keyword scans on the same raw text, with no shared computation. The domain classifier in production never sees SECURITY, API_CONTRACT, or ARCHITECTURE as typed predicates — it sees the raw words "auth", "endpoint", "design" and tries to match them independently.
> The fix needed: ClassifyDomainAsync should either call DevelopmentPromptCompiler.Compile first and pass the resulting predicates to DomainClassifierUnit, or the orchestrator should run the compiler once and feed the result to both the classifier and the router. The compilation result is already available from CompilePromptAsync — the ordering needs to swap so compile comes first, then classify from the compiled form.
> This is a new gap to record — call it A61.You said: SemanticCompiler29.SemanticCompiler29.RouteClassifier.ClassifyByKeywords these are not ILogicalUnits? Learning mechanism?4:07 PMClaude responded: Let me read before answering.Let me read before answering.Read RouteClassifier in fullRead RouteClassifier in fullNow the answer is complete.
>
> Correct concern. RouteClassifier is a plain service class — not an ILogicalUnit, not registry-resolvable, and has no learning mechanism connected to the DPO path.
> It has two modes. ClassifyByKeywords is a pure static keyword scan — hardcoded domain-to-keyword maps, no training, no weights, no adaptation. Classify(int[] predicates) is a KNN over a manually trained list of (predicate array, domain) pairs — the Train() method loads examples, but there is no call to that method anywhere in the production orchestrator path. PromptDomainClassifier.Classify calls DomainClassifierUnit.Classify which calls RouteClassifier.ClassifyByKeywords — the static path. The KNN path is never reached in production.
> So what should be happening instead: The single source of truth session established that DomainClassifierUnit in project 23 is the canonical ILogicalUnit for domain classification, resolvable from the registry at PromptDomainClassifierUnit.Role. That means a trained replacement can be registered and will be selected over the deterministic fallback. That design is correct and is in place.
> The gap is that DomainClassifierUnit.Classify still calls RouteClassifier.ClassifyByKeywords on the raw prompt — the same static scan, not the KNN trained path, and not the DevelopmentPromptCompiler predicate form. There are two things missing:
> First, DomainClassifierUnit should receive the compiled predicate ids from DevelopmentPromptCompiler as its input, not the raw string. The DomainClassifierRequest has a Predicates int array field for exactly this — but in the orchestrator, ClassifyDomainAsync runs before CompilePromptAsync, so predicates are never populated. The ordering needs to flip: compile first, classify from compiled predicates.
> Second, RouteClassifier.Train() is never called in production. The KNN classifier — the actual learned mechanism from E18 — is trained in the experiment but the trained instance is never persisted, loaded, or wired into DomainClassifierUnit. The DPO loop teaches domain adapters and sub-phase routing, but the domain classifier itself never improves from feedback. It is permanently frozen at ClassifyByKeywords.
> This needs a plan — A61. The fix is: swap the orchestrator ordering so CompilePromptAsync runs first, pass the resulting DevelopmentPredicateIds as the Predicates field on DomainClassifierRequest, and ensure DomainClassifierUnit.Classify uses the predicate-based KNN path when predicates are present. The RouteClassifier KNN instance also needs to be trainable from the DPO teaching loop so it improves as the system sees more prompts.

Because they are two different things:

`35.ExperimentsV2/GlobalUsings.cs` belongs in project 35. C# global usings are project-local compile aliases. That file is a compatibility shim so old experiment files can say `MethodKnnPredictor` while actually resolving to production classes from `12.SemanticCompiler`. Moving it to `00.Core` would not affect project 35, and it would be wrong for `00.Core` to alias higher-level production namespaces.

`35.ExperimentsV2/Core/` is badly named. It is not architectural core. It is experiment-harness core. It currently contains:

- `ExperimentV2Result` / `NgramResultEntry`: experiment report DTOs, should stay experiment-local.
- `ProbeNeuralNetwork`: experiment-only probe, should stay experiment-local unless promoted.
- `SparseNgramTable`: experiment helper, should stay local unless promoted.
- `SimdMatMul`: old E12 experiment helper; since SIMD was promoted to `00.TensorCore`, this should probably be deleted or redirected.
- `OperationResult<T>`: this one is a real duplicate and should not stay there long-term. Experiments should use the shared `00.Core`/`AgentInfrastructure.OperationResult<T>` envelope.

> Минимальный fix в LogicalDpoTrainingUnit:
> csharp// Вместо:
> var lastMetrics = trainer.StepVector(batches, 1);
> // ... DpoStepCount: 1
>
> // Нужно:
> var monitor = new ConvergenceMonitor(threshold: 0.002f, windowSteps: 25);
> DpoMetrics? lastMetrics = null;
> int step = 0;
> do
> {
>     step++;
>     lastMetrics = trainer.StepVector(batches, step);
>     if (cancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested) break;
> } while (!monitor.ShouldStop(lastMetrics.Loss) && step < maxSteps);
> // ... DpoStepCount: step
> maxSteps — из LogicalDpoTrainingRequest (новое поле) или константа (например 50). ConvergenceMonitor уже реализован (согласно сообщению), нужно только его подключить здесь.

`21.AgentInfrastructure` может знать **когда вызвать обучение** и как подключить результат к registry/flow/orchestrator.

Но `21.AgentInfrastructure` не должен содержать саму обучающую механику:

- convergence logic

Это должно жить в `16.AutonomousLearning` или отдельном проекте типа `18.CapabilityTraining`, а контракты должны быть в `00.Core`.

- `E35 DependencyGraph` в `22.AgentAlgorithms`

- flags/contracts в `00.Core`

> что это за показатель такой? < disk 52.15%, >

`disk 52.15%` — это **процент занятости всего диска C:**, не размер обучения и не размер модели.

То есть примерно:

```text
(C: total size - C: free space) / C: total size * 100
```

Он показывает общий фон машины: Windows, проекты, кэши, Avast, старые run folders, всё вместе.

Для самой загрузки XIIGen важнее два других показателя:

- `checkpoint_mb` — сколько весят чекпоинты текущего обучения. Сейчас было около `0.6 MB`.
- `run disk` / размер run folder — сколько занимает текущий запуск целиком.

Так что `disk 52.15%` означает: диск C занят примерно наполовину. До стоп-гейта `80%` далеко.

Да, похоже проблема реальная. Новые гайды говорят, что готовый teaching set должен быть DPO-pair DTO, а текущий internal set в основном является **source-row registry**, не полноценным DPO DTO.

Главные находки:

1. В trainer всё ещё живёт запрещённый rejected:
   [DefaultLogicalCapabilityTrainer.cs](/C:/Projects/llm_mvp_core/18.CapabilityTraining/DefaultLogicalCapabilityTrainer.cs:173)

```csharp
$"Do not generate a capability for sub-phase {subPhase.Value.SubPhase.SubPhaseId}."
```

То же самое есть в replay:
[LogicalExperimentOptimizations.cs](/C:/Projects/llm_mvp_core/18.CapabilityTraining/LogicalExperimentOptimizations.cs:172)

Это прямо нарушает новые гайды: rejected должен быть Type A/B/C с реальным wrong-scope ответом и `[WRONG: ...]`, а не negation template.

2. `rows-200-fixed.jsonl` содержит только источник:
`RowId`, `UserRequest`, `Domain`, `Predicates`, `TargetSubPhases`.

Но по новым гайдам там не хватает обязательных pair/DTO полей:
`contract_signature`, `pair_kind`, `rejected_type`, `compiled_prompt_in_training`, `[WRONG: ...]`, `overlap_ratio`, `annotation_quality`, `chosen`, `rejected`, Stage 9 corruption markers.

3. Runner сейчас превращает каждую строку в synthetic knowledge-edge branch:
[Program.cs](/C:/Projects/llm_mvp_core/experiments-v2/XIIGEN-DOCS-BATCH-COMPARISON/runner/XiigenDocsBatchComparisonRunner/Program.cs:515)

`FinalHumanResult` становится:

```text
XIIGen documentation teaching row {RowId}: {UserRequest}
```

Это не BUG DTO, не PLAN DTO, не ARCH DTO. Это просто generic teaching branch.

4. Очень важный конфликт: из `2792` строк `2143` имеют больше одного `TargetSubPhase`.
Новые гайды явно говорят: multi-route prompt нельзя использовать как single-subphase chosen для нескольких подфаз. А текущий `BuildBranches` делает именно это: один prompt размножается по всем `TargetSubPhases`.

5. Старые `full-active-source-training-sets/.../node-*.md` тоже не соответствуют новым DPO-гайдам. Они A/B-only, без rejected, без `[WRONG]`, без `rejected_type`, без compiled prompt gate. Их можно использовать как B-side/reference material, но не как готовые DPO pairs.

Итог: **да, стоит переделать sets**, но не выбрасывать source pool. Правильнее сохранить `rows-200-fixed.jsonl` как источник, а заново сгенерировать поверх него DPO pair files по новым DTO-правилам:

- BUG: wrong responsibility rejected, не другой правильный subphase того же prompt.
- PLAN: branch DTO с `depends_on`; rejected = wrong order / missing dependency.
- ARCH: boundary/design DTO; rejected = implementation/tooling/refactor confusion.
- Все: `[WRONG: ...]`, `rejected_type`, overlap gate, `compiled_prompt_in_training=true`.

Самое срочное перед любым новым teaching run: убрать negation rejected из trainer/replay, иначе даже хороший source set снова превращается в плохую DPO-пару.

> что скажешь об этих семействах?Читаю v5 registry чтобы знать что уже есть, потом сравниваю с этим списком.Хорошо. Разбираю каждое из 13 семейств по одному критерию: что из него можно сделать DPO парой и с каким overlap.
>
> ---
>
> **U01 — product_business_flow_specs** (BFA docs, task catalogs, engine architecture per business module)
>
> Частично покрыто Type 2. Проблема в том что эти документы содержат три разных вещи одновременно: архитектурные решения (→ Type 9), acceptance criteria (→ Type 8), и task type контракты (→ Type 5). Объединять их под Type 2 неправильно — каждая часть производит разный rejected. Acceptance criteria из BFA doc → ArbiterUnit пары. Task type контракты → routing пары. Архитектурные решения → ARCH Type A.
>
> **Вывод:** нужен явный тип с правилом разбивки на три зоны внутри документа. Не отдельный тип, но явная секция в Type 2 с zone mapping.
>
> ---
>
> **U02 — deep_research_reports** (external/domain research, marketplace research)
>
> Не покрыто. И правильно что не покрыто — это опасный источник. Эти документы описывают внешний мир ("рынок показывает X", "конкуренты делают Y") а не внутренние решения XIIGen. Chosen из них может оказаться устаревшим или неточным уже через месяц.
>
> DPO потенциал есть но ограниченный: только для CODE_Q пар где вопрос о внешнем домене ("как работает GraphQL federation"), и только когда документ цитирует конкретный внешний стандарт. Rejected = устаревшая или упрощённая версия того же факта.
>
> **Вывод:** добавить как отдельный тип с жёстким ограничением — только CODE_Q, только с внешней ссылкой как authority, никогда как ARCH или PLAN B-side.
>
> ---
>
> **U03 — translation_migration_plans** (NestJS→Python, Figma→React Native, TRANSLATION_STATE.json)
>
> Не покрыто. Высокий DPO потенциал — самый чистый источник PLAN Type B пар. Планы миграции содержат явный dependency ordering: "сначала core fabric interfaces, потом DNA patterns, потом factory layer". Rejected = тот же список в неправильном порядке. Overlap 0.35–0.50, но аннотация уже написана в самом документе ("X нельзя до Y потому что Y зависит от X").
>
> STATE.json файлы из этих миграций — отдельная ценность: они показывают что было сделано на каком шаге, что прерывалось, что переделывалось. Это коррекционные события в machine-readable форме.
>
> **Вывод:** отдельный тип. B-side authority для PLAN Type B. STATE.json → measurement evidence (ближе к Type 4).
>
> ---
>
> **U04 — plugin_extension_marketplace_docs** (Wordpress, Adobe, plugin plans)
>
> Частично покрыто Type 2. Настоящая проблема здесь другая: эти документы описывают внешние платформы которые XIIGen не контролирует. Chosen из них может быть "правильным для Wordpress" но неправильным для XIIGen's implementation contract.
>
> DPO потенциал низкий если использовать как authority. Высокий если использовать как A-side source — реальные разработческие промпты из plugin integration сессий ("как подключить Wordpress webhook к XIIGen flow") дадут хорошие CODE_Q и PLAN A-sides.
>
> **Вывод:** не отдельный тип. A-side prompts → Type 1. Planning documents → Type 2. Не использовать как B-side authority для XIIGen-specific decisions.
>
> ---
>
> **U05 — skill_library_docs** (SKILL.md, skill manifests, prompt templates)
>
> Не покрыто. Это очень специфичный источник. Skill документы описывают "как агент должен себя вести при задаче X" — это поведенческие инструкции, не технические решения. DPO пара из skill doc: A-side = задача которую skill решает, Chosen = поведение по skill, Rejected = поведение без skill или с неправильным skill.
>
> Overlap будет высокий если rejected просто "делает то же самое менее структурированно". Нужен Type C rejected — другой домен, не просто менее чёткий ответ.
>
> **Вывод:** отдельный тип, но с ограничением — только Type C rejected (wrong domain), не Type A. Skill doc определяет domain boundary, rejected нарушает его.
>
> ---
>
> **U06 — delivery_test_packages** (E2E plans, GATE-B-FINDINGS.md, learning-pipeline-test-plan)
>
> Частично покрыто Types 8 и 11. GATE findings — это дословно ArbiterUnit B-sides с реальными findings из production delivery. Это лучший возможный источник для Type 8 пар потому что findings реальные, не сконструированные.
>
> E2E test plans — источник для 5.2/5.3 sub-phase пар. "Как проверить что flow работает end-to-end" → TEST predicate → 5.2 or 5.3 chosen.
>
> **Вывод:** разделить на две части внутри одного типа: GATE findings → Type 8 extension, test plans → Type 5/10 extension. Не нужен отдельный тип — нужна явная зона внутри Type 8.
>
> ---
>
> **U07 — flow_portability_protocols** (FLOW-PORTABILITY-TEST-PROTOCOL, FORK-EXECUTION-DIRECTIVE)
>
> Частично покрыто Type 2/10. Но это действительно уникальная категория. Portability protocols определяют что должно быть верным для любого flow независимо от tenant — это invariants. DPO пара: Chosen = flow проходит portability check, Rejected = flow с hardcoded tenant assumption который нарушает check. Overlap 0.10–0.20, очень чистый.
>
> FORK-EXECUTION-DIRECTIVE — это runtime contract для разветвления flow. Источник для SchemePlannerUnit пар с explicit fork/join semantics.
>
> **Вывод:** заслуживает явного типа. Единственный источник invariant-based пар. Rejected конструируется механически: взять correct flow → добавить один tenant-specific hardcode → [WRONG: portability check X fails because...].
>
> ---
>
> **U08 — design_conversion_docs** (Figma→code, Adobe Express, UI conversion maps)
>
> Не покрыто. DPO потенциал минимальный для routing и orchestration training. Это UI/UX домен — предикат UI. Полезен только для 4.2 Frontend и 1.1 Design System пар.
>
> Реальная ценность здесь не в B-side authority а в A-side prompts: "convert this Figma component to React" — реальный developer prompt с UI predicate. Chosen = правильная React реализация следующая design system. Rejected = реализация игнорирующая design tokens.
>
> **Вывод:** не отдельный тип. A-side prompts → Type 1 (UI predicate). Design specs → B-side для 1.1/4.2 пар под Type 2.
>
> ---
>
> **U09 — machine_state_json** (STATE.json, TRANSLATION_STATE.json, xiigen-file-state.json)
>
> Частично покрыто Type 4. Разница важная: Type 4 — это DPO training metrics (loss, accuracy, checkpoint bytes). Эти STATE.json — это workflow execution state (что сделано, что pending, какие артефакты созданы). Разные вещи.
>
> Execution state JSONs → источник для ModelTrainingUnit и CorrectionLearningUnit B-sides когда нужно показать что правильная запись состояния выглядит так, а не иначе. Rejected = неполная запись (missing required fields) — точно как Type 11 логика но для execution state.
>
> **Вывод:** выделить как явную зону внутри Type 4, или создать Type 17 — "execution state evidence". Логика извлечения пар идентична Type 11 (missing fields = rejected).
>
> ---
>
> **U10 — source_archives_and_snapshots** (*.zip, xiigen_v18_complete.zip)
>
> Не покрыто и правильно что не покрыто. ZIP архивы — не документы, это упакованные артефакты. Содержимое архивов может содержать документы из других типов, но сам архив как единица — это delivery artifact, не source.
>
> DPO потенциал нулевой напрямую. Архив нужно распаковать и классифицировать содержимое по существующим типам.
>
> **Вывод:** добавить в Type 6 (excluded) с правилом: ZIP → распаковать → классифицировать содержимое → применить соответствующий тип. Сам ZIP файл не входит в обучение.
>
> ---
>
> **U11 — agent_tooling_instructions** (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, copilot-instructions.md)
>
> Частично покрыто Types 14/15. Разница реальная: Type 14 — behavioral rules для пользователя ("не делай X"). AGENTS.md и CLAUDE.md — инструкции для инструмента ("когда вызывать tool X", "как интерпретировать output Y"). Это machine-facing, не human-facing.
>
> DPO потенциал: источник для ArbiterUnit пар где arbiter проверяет правильно ли агент следует своим инструкциям. Chosen = агент вызывает правильный tool в правильном порядке. Rejected = агент пропускает обязательный шаг.
>
> **Вывод:** отдельный тип. Не Type 14 потому что audience другой. Принципиально — это executable contract, не behavioral rule.
>
> ---
>
> **U12 — capability_catalogs_and_matrices** (CAPABILITY_MATRIX.md, UNIFIED_SOURCE_INDEX, SKILLS_FACTORY_RAG)
>
> Не покрыто. Смешанная группа которую нужно разбить:
> - CAPABILITY_MATRIX → близко к Type 7 (что реализовано, что нет) — уже покрывается
> - UNIFIED_SOURCE_INDEX → reference material, не пары
> - SKILLS_FACTORY_RAG → RAG индекс для skills — vocabulary calibration, не B-side
>
> Единственная уникальная часть: матрицы покрытия ("flow X покрывает sub-phases Y, Z, не покрывает W") — источник для knowledge-edge detection пар. Chosen = KNOWLEDGE_EDGE для W. Rejected = PASS для W когда flow не зарегистрирован.
>
> **Вывод:** не новый тип. Capability matrix → расширение Type 7. RAG индексы и source indexes → Type 6 (excluded as direct pair source, vocabulary calibration only).
>
> ---
>
> **U13 — raw_merged_text_dumps** (extracted_merged.txt, planning session.txt)
>
> Частично покрыто. Правильное замечание в списке: "not safe as direct Type 1". Эти файлы — несегментированные конкатенации нескольких разговоров или документов. A-side из них без preprocessing будет содержать фрагменты из разных контекстов смешанные вместе.
>
> Единственно правильное использование: preprocessing pipeline — сегментировать по разделителям ("---", timestamps, "Human:", "Assistant:"), затем классифицировать каждый сегмент по существующим типам.
>
> **Вывод:** добавить в Type 6 (excluded until preprocessed) с явным preprocessing протоколом. После сегментации каждый фрагмент классифицируется заново.
>
